Une application belge pour toujours trouver le camion du glacier Unsplash. L’ idée lui est venue d’un vendeur de glaces flamand. « Il voulait une application pour que les gens puissent le suivre sur la route », explique Kristof Jochmans. Une demande qui faisait écho à une expérience personnelle. « Vous entendez le son du camion très tard, vous devez prendre de l’argent, demander à votre famille ce qu’elle veut, trouver vos chaussures… Et quand vous êtes enfin dehors, vous voyez le camion passer devant vous. Je me suis dit qu’il devait y avoir une meilleure solution. » Avec son entreprise de consultance, Kristof développe alors « Radar à glaces » . Cinq ans plus tard, l’application rassemble pas moins de 80 camions de glaces sur l’ensemble du pays et plus de 120.000 utilisateurs. Pour les glaciers, l’intérêt est très concret : éviter les clients manqués et générer des ventes en plus. Instagram DY2GHi9CEkC Lorsqu’un camion approche, les utilisateurs reçoivent une notification. « Les gens savent exactement quand ils doivent être dehors pour acheter leur glace. Ils ne manquent plus le camion », explique Kristof. Tous ne sortiront évidemment pas acheter une glace. « Mais quelques-uns vont le faire. Ce sont des ventes supplémentaires. » L’application permet aussi d’élargir la clientèle. « Les personnes qui habitent à 100 mètres de la rue où passe habituellement le camion peuvent maintenant venir sur la route principale parce qu’elles savent exactement quand elles doivent y être. » Et avec la fonction « Appeler le camion de glace », elles peuvent même demander au vendeur de se déplacer jusqu’à leur domicile, dans un rayon d’un kilomètre. « Il peut quitter sa route juste pour vendre, par exemple, cinq glaces. Et c’est toujours ça de pris. » « L’ancienne manière de vendre est en train de disparaître » Kristof Pour les glaciers, l’accès à l’application passe par un abonnement. « C’est un petit prix », précise Kristof, qui ne souhaite pas en révéler le montant. Révolution de l’organisation Mais l’outil ne se contente parfois plus d’accompagner le métier : il en modifie l’organisation. Kristof cite l’exemple d’un vendeur en Flandre qui a abandonné ses tournées classiques. « Quand il fait chaud, il va désormais de demande en demande. Il ne fait plus ses tours réguliers. » Une façon d’adapter ses déplacements à la demande réelle plutôt que de suivre un itinéraire fixe. On ne m’a jamais vraiment dit : ‘Non, nous n’en avons pas besoin.’ Pour Kristof, cette évolution annonce un changement plus profond. « L’ancienne manière de vendre est en train de disparaître et il faut passer à une solution digitale. » Une transition qui semble bien accueillie : « On ne m’a jamais vraiment dit : ‘Non, nous n’en avons pas besoin.’ Nous recevons beaucoup de retours positifs. » Kristof Jochmans. - DR Et parfois, ce sont même les clients qui font la prospection. « Nous avons beaucoup de personnes qui installent l’application et qui ne trouvent pas leur vendeur local. Elles lui disent ensuite : ‘Vous avez besoin de l’application !’ Et finalement, ce sont les glaciers qui nous contactent. » De quoi surprendre Kristof lui-même. « C’est un peu fou. Il y a McDonald’s, Quick, Uber Eats… et nous sommes là avec une petite application pour les commerces locaux. » Pourtant, « Radar à glaces » reste une activité parmi les produits développés par son entreprise. « Ce n’est pas mon travail à temps plein. » Pour son créateur, son développement ne fait toutefois que commencer. Avec des étés toujours plus chauds, la digitalisation pourrait bien devenir un nouvel outil de travail pour les glaciers et transformer leur façon de procéder. À l’origine de « Radar à glaces », il y a une frustration toute simple : celle de voir passer le camion de glaces au moment où l’on n’est pas prêt. Cinq ans plus tard, l’application développée par Kristof Jochmans, ne sert plus seulement à prévenir les gourmands. Elle commence aussi à transformer la manière dont certains vendeurs travaillent. Par Awatef Dourheri Le 14/08/2026 à 08:10 Références

Pourquoi la SNCB supprime plusieurs trains ce vendredi Image d’illustration. - BELGA. P lusieurs trains P (circulant aux heures de pointe) sont supprimés vendredi en raison des fortes chaleurs attendues durant la journée, avec des maxima allant jusqu’à 37 voire 38°C, indique la SNCB sur son site internet. L’entreprise ferroviaire conseille par ailleurs aux voyageurs d’éviter de prendre le train durant les heures de pointe et de toujours se déplacer avec de l’eau. Les trains P ne circulent pas en journée et n’effectuent qu’un trajet le matin et un autre le soir. Ils restent donc stationnés en plein air toute la journée et accumulent de la chaleur. Lorsque le thermomètre grimpe trop, ces véhicules ne peuvent donc pas circuler en toute sécurité pour les passagers et le personnel, d’autant plus qu’il s’agit souvent de trains plus vieux, qui ne disposent pas d’air conditionné, explique la SNCB pour justifier leur suppression. En outre, diminuer le nombre de trains qui circulent permet de réduire le risque que l’un d’entre eux se retrouve bloqué en pleine chaleur au milieu des voies. La SNCB ajoute que les caténaires se distendent sous forte chaleur, ce qui augmente le risque de cassure lors du passage des trains. The Iran War Has Left the U.S. Dangerously Exposed. The fight has offered Iran and other adversaries a clear picture of U.S. weaknesses.

Iran says US must meet its demands before Hormuz reopens. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until the United States meets its conditions, even as Tehran and Oman move closer to an agreement on a temporary shipping route.

Tehran rents hit three times many workers’ monthly pay. Average advertised monthly rent in Tehran has climbed above 720 million rials, roughly three times the earnings of many Iranian workers, exposing a widening affordability gap as some tenants face increases of up to 100%, market data showed in late July.

Iran’s healthcare crunch forces patients to cut treatment. Iranians are struggling to afford medicines and medical care, with some foregoing treatment as prices rise, drug shortages spread and insurance coverage falls short, according to accounts from patients.

Iran Supreme Court upholds protester's death sentence. Iran’s Supreme Court has upheld the death sentence of 28-year-old protester Rasoul Rezaei, who was arrested during nationwide protests in January, US-based rights group HRANA reported on Sunday.

Rezaei named Iran’s top security chief and Khamenei representative. Mohsen Rezaei was appointed as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s representative on Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on Sunday, before being named secretary of the powerful security body.

First red meat, now dairy: Iran’s household diet keeps shrinking. Soaring food prices are reshaping what Iranian families eat, with new figures showing a steep decline in dairy consumption alongside a longer retreat from red meat as household purchasing power erodes.

The strange power of Iran’s absent supreme leader. Mojtaba Khamenei’s continued absence from public view has created an unusual system of authority in Tehran, where decisions are made and justified through written messages attributed to him while responsibility appears dispersed across a core establishment network.

Iran’s Journalist Day comes amid arrests and prison terms. Iran marked its annual Journalists’ Day this week as reporters remained behind bars, others faced lengthy prison sentences and rights groups warned that a crackdown on independent reporting has intensified since nationwide anti-government protests erupted earlier this year.

From Karbala-4 to AMIA: Mohsen Rezaei returns to Iran’s security helm. Mohsen Rezaei, whose four decades in Iran’s ruling establishment span the disputed Karbala-4 offensive, repeated failed presidential campaigns and an Interpol Red Notice over the AMIA bombing, returned to a top security post on Sunday.
Iran arrests football fan-page operator after protest-themed posts. Iranian football fan-page operator arrested after club complaint

Khamenei fills six top military posts as key intelligence gaps persist. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointed six top military commanders Monday, formalizing parts of a wartime leadership structure that operated for months without decrees while leaving several sensitive intelligence posts without publicly named permanent chiefs.

Mojtaba Khamenei orders integration of Iran’s top military command bodies. Iran’s Supreme Leader on Monday ordered the completion of a process to integrate the Armed Forces General Staff with the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, Iran’s top operational military command, as he appointed Ali Abdollahi chief of staff.

Protest crackdown veteran Taeb returns to lead Basij, expand intel network. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointed veteran intelligence official Hossein Taeb to lead the Basij, giving the former protest crackdown figure a mandate to expand the paramilitary force’s grassroots intelligence network and use of new technologies.

Iran parliament advances Hormuz bill targeting US, Israeli transit. Iranian lawmakers are advancing a sweeping bill aimed at asserting greater control over the Strait of Hormuz, including restrictions on US and Israeli assets in a waterway through which about one-fifth of global oil and LNG supplies passed before the war.

Iran plays down Mecca Pact as regional security order shifts. Iranian officials and analysts are publicly playing down the threat posed by a new defense pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, even as some commentators warn Tehran against underestimating an emerging regional alignment.

Two years on, Pezeshkian’s presidency is a tale of survival. Masoud Pezeshkian may have a claim to being Iran’s unluckiest president, with his two years in office dominated by wars that have battered an already ailing economy to the point that keeping households above subsistence would count as an achievement.

Iranian workers report layoffs, months of unpaid wages. Workers across Iran’s mining, industrial and municipal sectors say they have gone months without full pay, while some employers have also cut staff, deepening pressure on households already struggling with rising living costs.

Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death for crimes against humanity. A Syrian court convicted former President Bashar al-Assad of crimes against humanity and sentenced him to death on Tuesday in a case over killings, torture and arbitrary detention during the government's crackdown on protests that began in 2011.

German embassy in Tehran keeps visa services suspended. Germany's embassy in Tehran remains on emergency operations because of the security situation in Iran, with its visa section closed to regular visitors and no regular visa appointments being issued, the German Foreign Office told Iran International on Tuesday.

Rising costs leave Iranians 'nothing' for a coffee. Rising living costs have forced many Iranians to give up cafes and restaurants, turning a once-routine form of leisure into an expense increasingly squeezed out by rent, food and healthcare, messages to Iran International say.

All Mojtaba's men: Old guard shapes Iran’s new order. Iran's unseen supreme leader has issued his first military decrees, raising a central question about the emerging order under Mojtaba Khamenei: is he tightening his grip on power, or relying on the old security establishment to shore up his authority?

Iran security forces targeted protester’s monarchist tattoo, then killed him. Iranian security forces shot protester Farid Ramezani during the January protests in Tehran, then targeted his Pahlavi crown tattoo as he lay wounded before killing him with a shot to the forehead, a source familiar with the case told Iran International.

The Kinglet’s rookie mistake: how an Iranian hacker was caught at US request. A Turkish-Iranian man arrested in Montenegro at the request of the United States spent years working as an asset of Iran's Intelligence Ministry after rising to become one of the country's most accomplished hackers, an Iran International investigation has found.

Iran hardliners tout offensive posture as Khamenei reshapes military command. Iran's latest military appointments are consolidating its command structure after the recent war, with hardliners portraying the reshuffle as a shift toward a more unified and offensive posture.

US strikes Iran-bound ship as mediators signal Hormuz breakthrough. The maritime confrontation around Iran widened Tuesday as US forces struck an Iran-bound vessel and Tehran-backed Houthis attacked a ship in Bab el-Mandeb, even as Pakistan and Qatar signaled progress in mediation over the Strait of Hormuz.

At least 916 executed in Iran since January - rights group. Iran has carried out at least 916 executions since the start of 2026, including 15 so far in August, the Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran said on Tuesday.

From Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb, conflict converges on vital shipping lanes. Six people were killed when Iran-backed Houthis attacked a vessel in Bab el-Mandeb, an escalation experts say reflects not a second front in the Iran war but two conflicts converging, as the Houthis pursue their own interests while adding pressure on Iran’s adversaries.

Oil slicks hit Qeshm mangroves and Oman coast in mounting war fallout. Oil has reached mangrove forests on Iran's Qeshm island while a separate vast slick spreads toward Oman's coast, raising fears of environmental damage in waters already disrupted by war.

New online poll suggests eight in ten would like to leave Iran. More than eight in 10 respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll said they would leave Iran if given the opportunity, reflecting deep frustration among those who took part over the country’s economic and social conditions.

When the language of home is no longer the language of life. The child understands every word her grandmother says in Persian. She answers in English. She can ask what's for dinner in her parents' language, but not describe her anxiety, her love or her future in it. She calls herself Iranian. Persian is no longer the language of her life.

US ship strike tests Tehran’s narrative of victory in Hormuz. A US strike on a container ship approaching an Iranian port has complicated Tehran’s narrative of a strategic victory against Washington over the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran loses ground in oil market as neighbors rebound. OPEC oil production continued its sharp post-war recovery in July, but Iran remained a notable exception, with output still around a quarter below pre-war levels and its oil revenues taking an even steeper hit.

Iran could prolong war to outlast Trump, IRGC adviser says. A senior adviser to the commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tehran could deliberately prolong the war until US President Donald Trump leaves office to wear down its adversaries and deter future attacks.

Canada says IRGC conscription alone no bar as Iranians face scrutiny. Canada says immigration applications are assessed individually in response to cases of Iranians who completed mandatory military service with the Revolutionary Guards receiving letters warning they could be deemed inadmissible on security grounds.

Over 150,000 disabled Iranians await nursing allowances. More than 152,000 people with severe disabilities remain on a waiting list for nursing care payments because of insufficient funding, the rehabilitation deputy of Iran’s State Welfare Organization said on Wednesday.

Security by design: why Tehran is tearing up cobblestones. Tehran's municipality is tearing up the cobblestones of the capital's historic pedestrian zones and laying asphalt, a change officials call traffic management and that architects and urban sociologists read as something older: the redesign of a city to make protest harder.

Iran hardliners see shift on US talks in Rezaei appointment. Mohsen Rezaei’s appointment as Iran’s new security chief has opened a battle over its political meaning, with ultra-hardliners portraying the removal of his predecessor as evidence that the balance in Tehran has shifted against advocates of negotiations with Washington.

Iran International's Negar Mojtahedi wins top Canadian journalism honor. Iran International's Negar Mojtahedi has won Canada's 2026 Bill Good Award, part of the Jack Webster honors regarded as western Canada's preeminent journalism awards, cited for reporting that bridged the gulf between the West and Iran, often at risk to her own safety.

Iran seals dozens of businesses in renewed hijab crackdown. Iranian authorities have sealed at least 42 cafés, restaurants, shops, sports clubs and other businesses across the country in the past three weeks, over compulsory hijab rules and what officials describe as violations of Islamic norms.

Iran province suspends plan for sharply higher petrol price. A plan to sell petrol at a much higher “refinery cost” rate in southern Kerman province was halted hours before it was due to begin, the provincial fuel distribution company said on Thursday.

Land routes cannot replace Iran’s blocked sea trade, chamber official warns. Replacing a single ship carrying essential goods to Iran would require about 2,500 trucks, a Chamber of Commerce official warned, saying land routes cannot offset the US maritime blockade and negotiations are the only realistic way to restore trade.

Caspian Sea hits 200-year low as Iran debates the treaty meant to divide it. The Caspian Sea is falling by as much as 20 centimeters a year and stands at its lowest level in two centuries, an Iranian environment official said, a warning that lands just as Tehran reopens the argument over how to divide a sea that is shrinking on all five of its owners.

Iranian forces used cultural sites, medical clinics in Alborz crackdown. Security forces used cultural venues and medical clinics as firing positions, ammunition stores and sites for holding bodies during Iran's January 2026 protest crackdown in Alborz province, according to material reviewed by Iran International.

How Iran’s Supreme National Security Council works, and who gets a vote. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council brings together the country’s most powerful officials, but its workings are less straightforward than its name suggests, as even its secretary, often dubbed Iran’s security chief, does not automatically have a vote.

Tehran’s reshuffle leaves no pragmatic opening. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s latest appointments to Iran’s top security and paramilitary institutions are not routine personnel changes but a reflection of his priorities for tighter control over the institutions directing war and domestic repression.

US vows 'indefinite' blockade as Iran signals offensive posture. The US-Iran standoff is hardening around the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington saying it can sustain maritime pressure indefinitely and Tehran signaling readiness for a prolonged confrontation and more offensive operations.

Iran lawmakers push back on regional monitoring of Hormuz. A dispute in Iran’s parliament over the terms for reopening the Strait of Hormuz is threatening to complicate negotiations in Muscat, as lawmakers challenge a proposed role for Oman and Pakistan in monitoring shipping through the waterway.

Iran crackdown grinds on with new wave of prison terms. Iranian courts have handed down a new wave of prison terms and other punishments against protesters, activists and citizens accused of national security offenses, as the judicial crackdown that followed January’s nationwide protests continues months later.

'Better than nukes'? Iran digs in on Hormuz as US deal nears end. Iran is doubling down on control of the Strait of Hormuz, with some in Tehran now arguing the strategic leverage it provides is more valuable than a nuclear weapon.

Democrats turn Iran war costs against Trump as midterms near. US Democrats appear to be sharpening their attacks on President Donald Trump over the economic fallout from the Iran war as rising fuel and household costs become an increasingly potent issue ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Maroc : le port de Dakhla peut-il répliquer le modèle de Tanger Med ?. Le futur grand port du sud marocain, dont le projet a été lancé par Mohammed VI, sort des eaux. Il devra s’imposer dans une desserte maritime continentale en perpétuelle redéfinition.

Au Congo de Denis Sassou Nguesso, les Russes d’Africa Corps opèrent à visage découvert. Les organes de propagande russes ont récemment rendu publique la formation par les « instructeurs » d’Africa Corps, de la Direction générale de la sécurité présidentielle (DGSP) du Congo-Brazzaville. Le dernier épisode d’une relation assumée. Décryptage.

Hervé Renard : « En Côte d’Ivoire, je suis là où je voulais être ». Onze ans après avoir quitté la Côte d’Ivoire, alors sacrée championne d’Afrique, le Français va de nouveau entraîner les Éléphants. Une proposition qui « ne se refuse pas », assure Hervé Renard dans cet entretien accordé à Jeune Afrique.

« Saroukh », « El Hamra », « Madame Courage » : ces psychotropes qui menacent l’Algérie. Plus de 44 millions de comprimés saisis en 2025, 28 voyageurs tués fin juillet dans un accident causé par un chauffeur de bus drogué, des consommateurs jusque dans les cours d’école… L’Algérie s’émeut et s’inquiète de la prolifération des psychotropes, qui gangrènent et menacent toute la société.

Guinée : que signifie le nouvel accord avec le FMI ?. Conakry s’apprête à obtenir 425 millions de dollars dans le cadre d’un accord avec le Fonds monétaire international. Au-delà des financements attendus, le programme doit surtout imposer un cadre de discipline pour gérer la rente minière et renforcer les finances publiques.

RDC : un début de décrispation politique, avant un dialogue national ?. Quelques signaux faibles laissent penser à un moment de détente du pouvoir après que le président, Félix Tshisekedi, s’est dit ouvert à l’organisation d’un dialogue national.

Cameroun : de Genève à Yaoundé, Samuel Mvondo Ayolo, gardien du temple Biya. Il est le directeur du cabinet civil de Paul Biya et, entre la Suisse, la France et le Cameroun, son bouclier pour contrer rumeurs et rivalités au sein du sérail. Portrait de Samuel Mvondo Ayolo, homme de l’ombre d’un président absent.

TotalEnergies, Eni, Shell… Comment la crise d’Ormuz profite aux majors, y compris en Afrique. Grâce à l’envol des cours et à la progression des marges de raffinage, les résultats financiers des géants des hydrocarbures sont en nette progression. Les cartes sont rebattues à l’échelle mondiale, et l’attractivité du continent augmente.

Côte d’Ivoire : Yacine Idriss Diallo unique candidat à la FIF, les clubs brandissent le boycott. La Fédération ivoirienne de football élira son président le 12 septembre, Yacine Idriss Diallo étant l’unique candidat, après des tractations gouvernementales. Mais la grogne couve chez les clubs, qui réclament plus de moyens.

Le Quai d’Orsay ouvre une procédure disciplinaire contre l’ambassadeur de France en Centrafrique. Dans un article paru ce mercredi, l’hebdomadaire Le Canard enchaîné affirme que Bruno Foucher a fait venir dans ses appartements privés de la résidence une trentaine de jeunes femmes entre janvier 2024 et mars 2026, poussant les services de protection à signaler une faille de sécurité.

Présidentielle en Zambie : duel dans les urnes entre Hichilema, favori pour un second mandat, et Mundubile, opposant sous pression. Favori des sondages, Hakainde Hichilema brigue un second mandat face à Brian Mundubile. Entre bilan économique contesté et réforme constitutionnelle controversée, le scrutin révèle les fractures politiques d’une démocratie sous tension.

RDC : autour de Tshisekedi, d’ultimes tractations en attendant la convocation du dialogue. Alors que plusieurs sources évoquent une possible prise de parole du président Félix Tshisekedi dans les prochains jours, ce dernier a réuni des représentants des Églises et les membres d’une commission spéciale pour évoquer les contours des futures assises.

Pétrole : pourquoi le Nigeria se tourne de plus en plus vers la mer. Pour échapper aux défaillances techniques de ses oléoducs terrestres et aux actes de sabotage qui les frappent dans le delta du Niger, la Nigerian National Petroleum Company privilégie les exportations de brut par voie maritime.

Maroc : Azrou, un collège au service d’une « politique berbère ». Conçu sous le Protectorat pour produire des cadres et auxiliaires acquis à la France, le collège berbère d’Azrou est devenu, malgré lui, un vecteur de mobilité sociale. Histoire d’une institution trahie par ses propres élèves, qui l’ont utilisée pour écrire leur histoire nationale.

De Brazzaville à Libreville, Omar Denis Bongo Ondimba à pas prudents vers la politique. Omar Denis Bongo Ondimba séjourne de plus en plus régulièrement à Libreville. Le petit-fils de Denis Sassou Nguesso et frère d’Ali Bongo Ondimba reste discret, mais entretient un flou stratégique autour d’un retour au Gabon et d’ambitions politiques.

Mali-Algérie : entre Assimi Goïta et Abdelmadjid Tebboune, les dessous d’une réconciliation inattendue. Après plus d’une année de tensions qui avaient abouti à une rupture diplomatique sans précédent, Bamako et Alger renouent le dialogue. Une normalisation fruit de plusieurs médiations, menées par la Russie, par le Niger et par le Congo.

Cameroun : ce qu’il faut savoir sur Hippolyte Ebaka, le vrai patron de l’armée. Paul Biya a nommé ce général de division au poste de major-général des armées. Si René Claude Meka reste chef d’état-major, la santé défaillante de ce dernier fait donc d’Hippolyte Ebaka le numéro un officieux de l’armée camerounaise.

Ethiopian Airlines : Mesfin Tasew, un DG devenu indispensable ?. Faute de successeur désigné, Mesfin Tasew reste à la tête d’Ethiopian Airlines pour une année supplémentaire. Un répit qui doit permettre au groupe de finaliser ses investissements record et de relancer la course à la succession.

Crise migratoire à Ceuta : le Maroc assure prendre « toutes les mesures nécessaires ». Les autorités marocaines ont annoncé, ce mercredi 12 août, mobiliser leurs forces pour tenter de contrer tout nouvel afflux de migrants vers l’enclave espagnole, après avoir constaté une nouvelle vague de désinformation sur les réseaux sociaux.

Mali : 10 choses à savoir sur Fatou Binta Diop, la discrète conseillère diplomatique d’Assimi Goïta. Fidèle parmi les fidèles du chef de la junte malienne, Fatou Binta Diop accompagne Assimi Goïta depuis sa prise du pouvoir. Conseillère spéciale chargée des questions diplomatiques, elle s’impose comme l’un des piliers les plus discrets, mais aussi les plus influents, du palais de Koulouba.

Mali-France : Assimi Goïta accorde une grâce à l’officier de la DGSE détenu depuis un an à Bamako. Yann V. a été gracié par le président de la transition malienne. L’agent des services de renseignement français était accusé par Bamako d’avoir participé à un complot visant à « déstabiliser les institutions de la République ». Selon nos informations, le Maroc est intervenu dans cet épineux dossier.

De la « poudre » à l’instruction, la fabrique d’une intelligentsia amazighe. Censé assigner à la jeunesse berbère une place précise dans l’ordre colonial, le collège d’Azrou échappe au destin imaginé par ses fondateurs. À mesure que le savoir leur ouvre de nouveaux horizons, ses élèves découvrent qu’il peut aussi leur permettre de franchir les barrières sociales et politiques. Ils deviendront les généraux, magistrats et gouverneurs du Maroc indépendant.

NSIA débauche le patron de Sunu Bank Togo pour diriger sa filiale ivoirienne. Changement de direction générale à NSIA Côte d’Ivoire, à partir du 1er septembre. Le groupe mise sur une personnalité dotée d’une double culture bancassurance – banque panafricaine pour accompagner son expansion régionale.

Côte d’Ivoire : Laurent Gbagbo distribue les postes, mais qui commande vraiment, au PPA-CI ?. Après avoir, en mai, révoqué tous les organes de son parti, Laurent Gbagbo a dévoilé, le 10 août, la nouvelle ossature du PPA-CI. Derrière une collégialité de façade, une structure complexe, taillée sur mesure pour assurer la prééminence du chef.

« Africa Corps Airline » : comment la Russie achemine armes et troupes au Sahel. Un rapport de l’ONG américaine C4ADS lève le voile sur la logistique aérienne d’Africa Corps. Sept compagnies, dont des opérateurs publics russes et africains, alimentent les bases au Mali, au Burkina Faso et au Niger.

Maroc : les promoteurs immobiliers en plein âge d’or ?. Addoha, Alliances, Résidences Dar Saada : l’immobilier marocain renoue avec la croissance. Portés par la Coupe du monde 2030 et l’aide directe au logement, les grands promoteurs du royaume affichent des bilans assainis et des carnets de commandes bien garnis.

Cameroun : comment la Sosucam a changé de mains. Alors que Somdia, filiale du groupe Castel, avait annoncé son retrait de la première sucrerie du Cameroun, un consortium local, comptant l’avocat Joseph Pagop Noupoué mais aussi Henriette Noutchougouin et William Nkontchou, reprend le flambeau.

« Oui, je le veux ! » : en RDC, Grâce Kutino, porte-voix d’un changement de Constitution. La ministre de la Jeunesse et de l’Éveil patriotique était à la tête de milliers de manifestants qui se disent favorables à l’adoption d’une Loi fondamentale qui réponde à leurs aspirations.

Le Cameroun peut-il redevenir une fédération ?. Le 14 août 1961, la Constitution fédérale du Cameroun était adoptée à Yaoundé. Depuis, la fédération a disparu et Paul Biya, au pouvoir depuis 1982, a toujours été le défenseur d’un État unitaire. Mais le débat sur le fédéralisme reste d’actualité.

Tchad : ce que l’on sait du conflit entre l’Autorité de lutte contre la corruption et l’Agence de sécurité de l’État. Des agents de l’ANSE ont interpellé plusieurs contrôleurs de l’AILC qui enquêtaient sur la gestion de la Société des hydrocarbures du Tchad. L’institution anticorruption soupçonne que l’intervention soit liée à une autre affaire, impliquant le frère du patron des renseignements.

Une violente collision entre deux bus au Niger fait au moins 22 morts dont 17 militaires. Le drame est survenu au moment où les autorités nigériennes tentent d’enrayer la hausse des accidents de la route, qui ont fait plus de 1 200 morts dans le pays en 2025, selon les chiffres officiels.

Au Sénégal, le long combat des héritiers d’El-Hadj Omar Tall pour le retour du « trésor de Ségou » pillé sous la colonisation. Le guide spirituel soufi, dont les disciples se comptent par centaines de milliers, était un érudit et un combattant anticolonialiste du XIXᵉ siècle. L’adoption par la France, en avril, d’une loi sur les restitutions des biens culturels volés pourrait permettre à ses descendants de récupérer ses manuscrits, bijoux et biens de valeur.

Le pape Léon XIV appelle à l’ouverture de couloirs humanitaires au Soudan. « J’exhorte la communauté internationale à soutenir les efforts visant à instaurer un cessez-le-feu immédiat », a déclaré le souverain pontife, au sujet d’un conflit qui a fait des dizaines de milliers de morts et déplacé des millions de personnes.

La Guinée demande à la France la restitution du crâne de Bokar Biro, résistant à la colonisation française. Conakry entend récupérer les crânes du dernier souverain de l’Etat théocratique du Fouta-Djallon et de trois de ses proches, près de cent trente ans après leur assassinat par les troupes coloniales françaises.

Les étudiants marocains touchés de plein fouet par la hausse des frais d’inscription en France. Un décret, pris le 19 mai, restreint les possibilités d’exonération des droits d’inscription différenciés pour les étudiants non européens. Parmi eux, les Marocains sont les plus nombreux à étudier dans les facultés françaises.

« Ebola se propage à une vitesse que nous n’avions encore jamais observée » : l’alerte de Jean-Jacques Muyembe, codécouvreur du virus. Le virologue congolais, qui a mis au jour le virus en 1976, revient, dans un entretien au « Monde », sur l’actuelle propagation de l’épidémie due à Ebola en République démocratique du Congo. En seulement trois mois, le nombre de morts s’approche du bilan humain de l’épidémie de 2018, qui avait duré vingt-deux mois.

Au Maroc, la fin du démarchage téléphonique vers la France menace plus de 40 000 emplois. Une loi adoptée en France interdit toute prospection sans accord explicite du client à partir du 11 août. Elle met en danger des dizaines de milliers de salariés dans les centres d’appels marocains, largement dépendants du marché hexagonal.

Ebola : l’épidémie a fait plus de 2 000 morts en RDC. Ce bilan rapproche l’épidémie actuelle de celle qui avait sévi entre 2018 et 2020, la plus meurtrière à ce jour en République démocratique du Congo avec près de 2 300 morts.

En Somalie, la moitié des enfants déplacés dans les camps du sud-ouest souffrent de malnutrition aiguë. La sécheresse qui sévit en Somalie a provoqué le déplacement de dizaines de milliers de personnes. Dans les camps de déplacés, l’ONG Médecins sans frontières affirme faire face à « une augmentation alarmante du nombre d’enfants mal nourris admis depuis janvier ».

Au Kenya, le gouvernement veut réconcilier sa jeunesse avec l’agriculture. Le secteur, qui représente 22,5 % du produit intérieur brut kényan, est délaissé par les jeunes : l’âge moyen des exploitants est de 64 ans. Alors que la sécurité alimentaire du pays est en jeu, Nairobi promeut les métiers de la filière agricole.

Un mariage à 20 millions de dollars, symbole du clientélisme au Zimbabwe. Le président et tous les membres du gouvernement, ainsi que les hommes les plus riches du pays, ont assisté, en mai, aux noces du fils du principal magnat du Zimbabwe et conseiller présidentiel, Kudakwashe Tagwirei.

Bruno Foucher, l’ambassadeur de France en Centrafrique, visé par une procédure disciplinaire du Quai d’Orsay. Le diplomate a fait venir dans ses appartements privés de la résidence une trentaine de jeunes femmes entre janvier 2024 et mars 2026, poussant les services de protection à signaler une faille de sécurité, selon « Le Canard enchaîné ». Il reconnaît avoir eu des relations sexuelles avec deux d’entre elles.

« Le français fait désormais partie du patrimoine intellectuel, scientifique et culturel de l’Algérie ». Un collectif d’intellectuels et de citoyens algériens ou issus de la diaspora s’inquiète, dans une tribune au « Monde », de la marginalisation progressive du français au profit de l’anglais, davantage pour répondre à des considérations idéologiques qu’à une véritable stratégie linguistique cohérente.

Soudan : des frappes de drones visent Khartoum et deux autres villes du nord du pays après des mois d’accalmie. Cette attaque, mercredi à l’aube, semble coordonnée par les paramilitaires des Forces de soutien rapide, après plusieurs mois de calme relatif dans la guerre qui les oppose, depuis avril 2023, à l’armée soudanaise.

Zimbabwe : au moins 44 morts dans le chavirage d’un ferry sur le lac Kariba. D’une capacité de 90 personnes, le bateau comptait à son bord cinq membres d’équipages et 114 passagers adultes, selon le service de secours national. Les opérations de secours ont été compliquées par le mauvais temps.

Human Rights Watch says UN must keep peacekeepers in Lebanon Human Rights Watch has called on the United Nations to keep an international force in Lebanon after its peacekeepers' mandate ends this year. 'Agility vs depth': How the Mecca pact stacks up against the UAE-Israel alliance Submitted by Sean Mathews on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 18:55 Israel and the UAE have transactional ties based on military and intelligence sharing, but the Mecca pact has political depth Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, left, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, centre, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif meet in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on 7 August 2026 (Handout/Turkish presidency's press office/AFP) Off This summer, a senior UAE diplomat, Lanna Nusseibeh, held consultations with a US ally in Europe. The meeting was unremarkable but informative because of the impression the European country's officials walked away with. “The UAE is totally aligned with Israel. It’s crystal clear that the partnership has no limits,” a European official who was in the meeting told Middle East Eye. That clarity contrasts with the questions swirling in corridors of power - from the US to Asia - about the Mecca Agreement, which unites Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan under a mutual defence pact that many see as rivalling the UAE-Israel partnership . Western and Arab officials are still trying to decipher just how aligned Saudi Arabia , Pakistan and Turkey are, let alone whether they can back each other up in a hot conflict. For example, no sooner had the ink on the Mecca pact dried than the Houthis in Yemen attacked Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery. Pakistan and Turkey did not come to Riyadh’s defence against the Iran-aligned group. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In contrast, when the UAE came under attack from Iranian drones and missiles earlier this year, Israel dispatched Iron Dome air defence batteries to the Gulf state. Abu Dhabi also joined Israel in launching hundreds of strikes on Iran. “Israel did the UAE a big solid during the war. Abu Dhabi is not going to forget that,” a US official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity. But there are key differences between the two blocs. Despite the UAE and Israel’s military cooperation, their relations are still kept behind closed doors. "At first glance, the UAE-Israel bloc delivers more tangible gains for both parties, but the Mecca pact may ultimately resonate more broadly and less transactionally,” Theodore Singer, a former US intelligence officer, told Middle East Eye. 'The Mecca club can be expanded' When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that he visited the UAE at the height of the war on Iran, Abu Dhabi moved to deny the official statement. To many, that awkward diplomacy underscored just how unpopular the alliance remains outside Israeli and American circles. 'The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it” - Ayham Kamel, geopolitical analyst In contrast, the Mecca pact was celebrated in public. It was announced that Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan joined together for Friday prayer in the holiest city in Islam. The UAE and Israel have cooperated for decades. Their ties were given a public cloak in 2020 when Abu Dhabi officially recognised Israel under the Abraham Accords brokered by the US. They are united by their animosity towards Iran on one side and the Muslim Brotherhood on the other. Abu Dhabi’s escalating rivalry with Saudi Arabia, which has refused to recognise Israel, could give the two another point of agreement. The Abraham Accords have also solidified support in Washington for the UAE’s ruling Al-Nahyan family, even as the Emirates has hedged against the US with countries like China. But some analysts say the alliance between the UAE and Israel lacks depth. In some ways, the Mecca pact is its foil. “The UAE-Israel alliance is a political pact, but in reality, it’s the military and intelligence elements that define it,” Ayham Kamel, a geopolitical advisor on the Middle East, told MEE, referring to the Abraham Accords. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “The Mecca pact’s foundation is military, but it carries a lot of political meaning,” Kamel added, noting the agreement’s supposed foundation on a Nato-like Article 5 defence commitment. A lack of strategic depth is actually a physical reality for Israel and the UAE. The latter is expanding a military base in Somaliland that some officials in the Horn of Africa tell MEE could be used by Israel, but Somaliland is recognised only by Israel. Israel enjoys especially close ties with Greece . Both Israel and the UAE have growing military and economic ties with India and Ethiopia. But there are only one million Emirati nationals and 10.2 million Israelis. Few of their neighbours want to partner with Israel. Distrust of Israel has only grown in the wider Muslim world as a result of Israel's war on Gaza, which the United Nations and dozens of human rights groups have deemed a genocide . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “The UAE-Israeli cooperation is more agile and gets things done. The Mecca pact is going to move slowly and take time, but it has a public support base,” Kamel told MEE. “And the club can be expanded”. On paper, at least, the Mecca pact is formidable. 'Different threat perceptions' Turkey boasts the second-largest army in Nato, Saudi Arabia is the Arab world’s only G-20 economy, and Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim country. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have effectively been allies for decades. The kingdom provided financial support to Islamabad as it was acquiring a nuclear weapon. Pakistani pilots and officers have long filled the ranks of the kingdom’s military. In return, the Gulf state has provided a financial lifeline to Islamabad. But the two face different threats. UAE and Israel established fund for joint defence acquisition, sources say Read More » Saudi Arabia generally sees Iran as a more serious threat. In 2015, Saudi Arabia allied with the UAE to fight against the Houthis in Yemen. Pakistan decided against military involvement. Its more cordial ties to Tehran have positioned it as a mediator. Meanwhile, until a few years ago, Turkey and Saudi Arabia were at loggerheads over the Muslim Brotherhood. In Egypt, Saudi Arabia backed Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, who came to power in a coup that overthrew Egypt’s late president, Mohamed Morsi, who was democratically elected, and an ally of Erdogan Ties between Riyadh and Ankara hit rock bottom in 2019 when Turkey leaked audio tapes exposing the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi at Saudi Arabia's embassy in Ankara. It is only recently that Turkey and Saudi Arabia have converged in hotspots like Syria and Sudan. “The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey alignment is more complex, given that each operates in different regional environments and their perceptions of threat also differ considerably. It will take a lot of energy, effort and political will for the three states to find a way of working together and finding interoperability,” Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow and Gulf expert at Chatham House, told MEE. The war on Iran has only deepened ties between Israel and the UAE. MEE revealed in May that the two countries established a joint fund for defence acquisitions. Quilliam called the Israeli-UAE bloc “more actionable”. “The relationship has had time to bed in and has passed through many tests since the Abraham Accords were signed, and we have seen the two countries draw closer since the Israel-US war against Iran started,” he added. Which alliance has better interoperability? Turkey said on Thursday that its new allies will hold ‌joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation. The latter is a key goal for Ankara, which is pitching its drones and other weapons systems across the Middle East. The US and Turkey are Nato allies, while Saudi Arabia has long relied on the US as its main weapons supplier. Pakistan and Turkey have co-produced small warships, known as corvettes, as well as the Kaan fighter jet. They are working to produce Turkish anti-tank missiles. Saudi Arabia wants a local defence industry. 'The UAE has primarily US-systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems' - Elizabeth Dent, Washington Institute for Near East Studies But deep integration could pose a challenge. Pakistan’s main military supplier is China. Turkey wants to sell the Kaan fighter jet it is developing to Saudi Arabia, but the kingdom is eyeing the F-35. US officials tell MEE that Riyadh is unlikely to buy both. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia cannot match the intensity of Israel's defence cooperation with the US. The former’s military advantage is written into US law. Israel is openly lobbying against Saudi Arabia acquiring F-35s. “The Israelis have a broad defence industrial base, vast intelligence apparatus and battle-proven air and missile defence that is integrated via the US-led regional security order," Elizabeth Dent, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy and a former Pentagon official focused on the Gulf, told MEE. “The UAE has primarily US systems that are interoperable with Israeli systems, and have the money and regional prowess,” she added. Still, some analysts say that the very fact that Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have publicly codified their agreement gives it room to grow, potentially in ways the UAE-Israel alliance is unable to. The Mecca pact "contains a lot more strategic depth and binding commitment on mutual defence which could ultimately provide a more credible deterrent,” Dent said. “But the countries aren’t already integrated, so they have a long way to go”. Christopher Nolan remakes 'The Odyssey' as an Anglo-American imperial fantasy Submitted by Hamid Dabashi on Mon, 08/10/2026 - 05:40 Homer's epic emerged from the eastern Mediterranean, but Hollywood's latest adaptation continues a long tradition of appropriating ancient Greece for an invented western identity Matt Damon, Christopher Nolan and Anne Hathaway attend the New York premiere of 'The Odyssey' at AMC Lincoln Square Theater on 14 July 2026 (Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images via AFP) On By sheer serendipity, I watched Christopher Nolan's new film, The Odyssey , far from the madding crowd of Hollywood hype, in a small Greek town called Markopoulo Mesogaias. A historic little municipality in the East Attica region of Greece, it is a 15-minute ride from the temple ruins of the fifth-century BCE Sanctuary of Artemis at Vravrona (ancient Brauron), dedicated to the goddess of wild nature and childbirth. Artemis is also the name of the cinema where we sat to see Sir Christopher Nolan's new film, located right behind the splendid Saint John Orthodox Church of Markopoulo, built in 1904. You can't get more Greek than this! We sat there with about two dozen local Greeks in a splendid theatre, nowhere near the Imax hyperbole marketed through millions of dollars in advertising, trying to turn the film into a historic spectacle. Entirely unfazed by the grand hoopla, this little cinema in this little Greek town actually gave an old-fashioned "intermission" in the middle of the film, for bathroom breaks and popcorn. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); There and then, Nolan's obsession with size and magnitude was cut down to human scale: the spectacle was made to behave, brought down from its mightier-than-the-Trojan-Horse heights and forced to smell truth and reality. Nolan's juvenile obsession with the size of his Imax camera is a Trojan Horse. We should not take it to heart. Upon my return to New York, just to make sure, I saw the film at the largest Imax cinema in the city, as I had with all his previous spectacles. I infinitely prefer what I saw in that little Greek town - it was real. Whose Homer? Do Homer and his two classical masterpieces, the Iliad and the Odyssey , belong to the people with whom I sat in a dingy theatre in Markopoulo and watched Nolan's Odysseus? Or do they belong to a manufactured classical antiquity, code-named "the West", which a whole generation of European racist scholars, like the Austrian Jakob Philipp Fallmerayer (1790-1861), invented for themselves? Through that deliberate ideological project, contemporary Greeks were systematically alienated from their own linguistic, literary and philosophical heritage. All of this was done by way of rewriting the fact of Greece as the fictional foundation of "western civilisation", while actively erasing its geographical, historical and cultural ties to its own natural habitat in Asia Minor - in Anatolia, where Greece, Turkey , the Levant, Egypt and North Africa form a far more rooted historical truth. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); This treacherous ideological manoeuvre - the same one at the root of the racist thuggery of white supremacists like Elon Musk - has robbed Greece of its legacy, taken it literally stone by stone to the British Museum or the Louvre, to serve modern colonial and Eurocentric agendas, fabricating a thing that never existed. Nolan's film is entirely in the domain of this massive project of cultural appropriation - Europeans finding themselves a classical antiquity for their manufactured cultural authenticity The infamous Fallmerayer thesis claimed modern Greeks were not related to the ancient Hellenes, arguing that the population had been completely replaced by Slavic and Albanian migrations - as if any such migrations to any land were wrong, or exclusive to Greece. They liked the ancient Greeks and their arts and philosophy, and colonised them for themselves - textually and archaeologically stole and museumised them. A significant project of decolonising Greek cultural history - reclaiming it for the Greeks themselves - has long been at work. Nolan's take on Homer's Odyssey pulls in the opposite direction: it is integral to the prolonged cultural appropriation project of which Hollywood has been a mighty Trojan Horse. The fact is that Homer was not British, American or German. He lived in the eighth century BCE in the region of Ionia, on the western coast of Asia Minor, in modern-day Turkey. However you slice it, he would be far more at home in the lovely little theatre in the small Greek town where I saw Nolan's Odysseus than he would be anywhere in western Europe or North America. Nolan's film, judging by the plethora of praise it has garnered, is entirely in the domain of this massive project of cultural appropriation - Europeans finding themselves a classical antiquity for their manufactured cultural authenticity. Is it accidental, then, that Nolan's Odyssey features only one confirmed actor of Greek descent in its massive ensemble cast - Michael Vlamis , who is of Greek, Serbian and Lebanese ancestry, and who appears in a brief supporting role? The rest are mostly Hollywood, Los Angeles County, homegrown boys and girls of the Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway type. The limitations of these actors, Damon's in particular, could not possibly be unknown to a gifted and perfectionist filmmaker like Nolan. So why would he give his Odyssey such a palpably American and British - Anglo-American, as they say - look and feel? Unless this is precisely his purpose: to produce a decidedly Anglo-American Odyssey for our own time. The film's diverse supporting cast has meanwhile drawn fire from the opposite direction: Musk generated much nonsense when objecting to Lupita Nyong'o being cast as Helen. But such choices are entirely within the purview of studio executives seeking to cover all demographic bases for their own financial reasons - whereby we see the British-Indian actor Himesh Patel cast as Eurylochus, John Leguizamo as Eumaeus, Lupita Nyong'o as both Helen of Troy and Clytemnestra, and the transgender actor Elliot Page as Sinon. These are not "politically correct" decisions. These are financially opportune choices to touch base with various demographic audiences - which is why Nolan and his stars Damon and Tom Holland went to Mumbai on 10 July 2026 to promote their film in a vastly populated market where Himesh Patel is a known commodity. Imperial cinema It is not exactly a secret that I am not a fan of Nolan's cinema. The louder the propaganda his studios and the launch for each of his new films, the more suspicious and dismissive of his cinema I become. Despite the enormous positive and occasionally negative spin around his version of the Odyssey , I kept my peace until I actually saw the film. The propaganda machinery spinning the film intentionally amplified Musk's racist reaction to increase its appeal to precisely the demographic landscape the production studios had originally targeted. If I were to fall for all the hype Hollywood studios generate around every new film, then what would be the use of all those years I spent teaching Adorno and Horkheimer's groundbreaking idea of mass media as mass deception ? (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Forget about the Odyssey or Oppenheimer for a moment, and ask yourself about Nolan's fixation with time and memory in his other films - Memento (2000), Inception (2010), Tenet (2020) - where his fans think he is crafting "cinematic time machines" through mind-bending narratives to show how time and memory define identity. Why would he do that, and to what effect? What an astounding hubris, to take the very elemental force of time to task! The French phenomenologist Paul Ricoeur conducted a rigorous philosophical inquiry into the matter in his pioneering three-volume Time and Narrative (1983-1985). For any serious curiosity, we can just go there. In Nolan's hands, time and memory have a whole different purpose and texture. His take is the most astoundingly arrogant wish to colonise time and subjugate the mimetic registers of our working memories. Time, memory and being - the very stuff of which our fragile and vulnerable lives are made - he wishes to command and control, manipulate, massage and reorder in the living memory of a protagonist with whom no ordinary human being could possibly identify. Remember the Project for the New American Century (PNAC), the neocon chicanery that wanted to designate an entire century as "American" (by which they meant Israeli ) - namely, to lay claim to the very measure of time and memory? Nolan's cinema, like Samuel Huntington's " Clash of Civilisations " thesis, Francis Fukuyama's "End of History" idea and Benjamin Netanyahu's " Greater Israel " insanity, is part of the same demented and diseased way of imperial thinking. By concentrating on Odysseus's PTSD, the film is in fact pro-war, not anti-war. It deeply humanises the warmongers while dehumanising their victims Nolan's cinema of time and memory is the ideological foregrounding and aftereffect of PNAC. They both fume and fumble, but ultimately fail. To confess the obvious: my thinking on cinema is the product of the masters of world cinema - the exact opposite of the Hollywood blockbusters towards which I have an allergic aversion, despite the fact (or perhaps precisely because) I have in the past been a consultant to renowned Hollywood directors, and have some sense of how they work. I am most at home with the cinema of the masters of the art: Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray, Abbas Kiarostami, Nuri Bilge Ceylan, Elia Suleiman and Ousmane Sembene, among scores of other visionaries. The cinemas of Quentin Tarantino and Christopher Nolan I particularly dislike, for in every frame, every shot and every sequence of their films - in every superstar character they make, in the very tenor of their filmmaking - they carry the arrogance and conceit of their respective imperialisms up their sleeves. Nolan basks in and flaunts the power and wealth of pulling off a film of this magnitude. Every time I see this much power and arrogance, I run for cover. I was born and raised on the Soviet formalism of Sergei Eisenstein, and on the Italian neorealism of Roberto Rossellini, Vittorio De Sica, Luchino Visconti and others. Give me a single glorious shot of La Strada (1954) or Bicycle Thieves (1948) in exchange for the entirety of these arrogant, in-your-face, over-manly shots of Nolan and Tarantino. Give me a single shot of the Apu Trilogy (1955-1959), and I live happily without ever glancing at so much unbridled pomposity. Give me a single shot of Tokyo Story (1953) or Ran (1985), and I will forgo the entirety of Nolan's affected imperial filmmaking. The Imax spectacle They say Nolan's Odyssey is anti-war. I don't think so - and even if it were, it would be anti-war from the perspective of a nuclear-powered white-saviour fantasy. People around the globe do not like such fantasies, and find them entirely offensive. Nolan's Odysseus has PTSD: having first come up with the idea, then built the Trojan Horse, then caused the slaughter of his enemies, he has nightmares recalling what he has done - which is exactly how his Oppenheimer worked. First you cause and stage the mayhem and murder of fragile humanity at your mercy; then you go and make a film about the traumas of the mass murders you have inflicted upon the world. Israel is a master of this kind of cinema, with films such as Lebanon (2009), Waltz with Bashir (2008), and Beaufort (2007). The world must first endure Israel's criminal atrocities, and then have sympathy for the perpetrators when they have nightmares remembering what they have done to human beings. By concentrating on Odysseus's PTSD, the film is in fact pro-war, not anti-war. It deeply humanises the warmongers while dehumanising their victims. It focuses on the hero's psychological trauma, not on the transmutation of his murderous arrogance into hubris. To be sure, Nolan is entitled to his version of the Odyssey , as is any other reader of Homer's epic. The excellent scholar and Odyssey translator Emily Wilson is barking up the wrong tree: a film must be judged as a film, not by the English translation of a Greek original. Oppenheimer: The glorification of mass murder – coming to a cinema near you Read More » The problem is the overbearing bravura propaganda seeking to make Nolan's film into a unique cinematic event - which it certainly is not. Why would I, or any other sane human being, leave the glorious masterpiece of the late Greek master Theo Angelopoulos - Ulysses' Gaze (1995), a bold and brilliant take on Homer's epic - to come and be beholden to this gargantuan, one-eyed Polyphemus of an Imax camera developed for Nolan's production, and try to see the world from that frightful perspective? Audiences enter Imax theatres like Odysseus's comrades: once trapped there in darkness, they cannot wait to escape from a cave where they are transformed into food for Nolan's insatiable ego, acting like a man-eating Cyclops with his one-eyed camera. To watch this, as with all of Nolan's films, is to enter the opulent palace of a rich and arrogant British lord showing off his wealth and power. I don't like it - and I don't wish to be there. Imagine the power and wealth at your disposal: that you can have a new Imax camera developed for your production, to make a film that is supposed to defy the logic and rhetoric of the digital age and CGI, and feign reality! And then to do what, exactly, with that technology and that manufactured reality? Lionise Odysseus as a prototype of European imperialism, through one of the most racist, pro-war and reactionary readings of Homer's Odyssey ? All of that for what? So that every single human being entering that theatre, sitting in front of that gigantic screen while the creatures that come out of it speak colloquial American English like gods and immortals, should feel - frail, fragile and mortal as we are - smaller than a dispensable sailor at the mercy of the Cyclops? I have read countless reviews by professional film reviewers, one more awash and mesmerised than the other, beholden to this deeply anti-human spectacle deliberately designed so that everyone sitting in front of that gigantic screen would feel smaller than dust. This is obscene. No doubt we should feel like dust, as master poets like Omar Khayyam taught us, in the face of the fragility of life and the uncertainty of the purpose of our very existence. But what superior poetry, wisdom or philosophy does an unabashedly British imperialist, piggybacking on American imperialism, have to share with us fragile mortals? Absolutely nothing. Odyssey and colonialism Generations of postcolonial scholars have read the Odyssey as a foundational text of "proto-colonialism", in which the coloniser's gaze is cast on unfamiliar lands and indigenous peoples, who are subjugated and treated like savages and cannibals. But more humanely, Odysseus can be read as a refugee fleeing a war-torn land in search of his home, carrying the trauma of exile, forced migration and the disorientation of the diaspora. Nolan's Odysseus is far more the former than the latter. Against all such infinitely superior readings of Homer's epics, Nolan opts for the most prosaic white supremacist reading Consider, for example, Omeros (1990), the epic poem in which the Saint Lucian poet and playwright Derek Walcott recasts Homer's story in the postcolonial Caribbean, exploring the African diaspora and the trauma of the transatlantic slave trade, where displaced people are forced to redefine the concept of "home". In the same vein, Toni Morrison's novel Sula (1973) has been read as a postcolonial subversion of the epic hero's journey, centring the experience of African American women. Equally related is Suzan-Lori Parks's 2014 epic drama Father Comes Home From the Wars (Parts 1, 2 & 3) , which adapts Homer's Odyssey to explore the African American experience, following an enslaved Texan named Hero who is promised his freedom if he joins his master to fight for the Confederacy during the American Civil War. Against all such infinitely superior readings of Homer's epics, Nolan opts for the most prosaic white supremacist reading, precisely as his Batman trilogy opts for the demonisation of the Wall Street uprising, as indeed his Interstellar (2014) is a dangerous fantasy of US planetary colonialism. Greek voices For those who have never seen a Theo Angelopoulos film, watching one is like seeing the source of light in Plato's allegory of the cave - the best metaphor for Nolan's obsession with Imax and the cave-like theatre it creates for his audiences. Consider his absolute masterpiece, Ulysses' Gaze , a war drama also based on Homer's Odyssey . Without giving away too much, it is worth sitting down with one quiet evening at home, simply to marvel at the way a caring and competent Greek filmmaker turns a Greek literary masterpiece into a cinematic meditation on the history of his homeland, his continent and, through them, our world. The result is a profoundly meditative reflection on the genocidal massacres in the Balkans. Was there a genocide underway as Nolan was shooting his Odysseus , to which he might perhaps have referred? The Mediterranean Sea, the scene of Homer's Odyssey , is today the site of perilous journeys of a vastly different kind: African immigrants boarding sinking boats to reach a livable life; courageous activists boarding flotillas to reach Gaza and save its people from Israeli-imposed starvation , only to be kidnapped and raped by Israeli forces; and Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump trying to take over a whole island to "develop" it for other insanely rich parasites like themselves. How the Gaza genocide is redefining world cinema Read More » There is no sign of the real Mediterranean Sea in Nolan's testosterone-infested, adolescent take on the Odyssey . Angelopoulos is not the only one who will give you a superior reading. The Greek Nobel laureate George Seferis considered Homer not a relic of the past but the living voice of our world. He, too, used Homeric myth to frame the trauma of modern Greek history, in his Log Book trilogy (1940-1955), which uses the form of a ship's log to explore exile and identity against the Mediterranean landscape during times of war and turmoil. Another example is The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel (1938), the epic poem by the Greek poet, philosopher and novelist Nikos Kazantzakis, again based on Homer's epic. Other examples abound in the works of James Joyce, Margaret Atwood and others. Nolan's Odyssey is neither the best nor the worst take on the original, and must be placed in the context of countless other takes on a literary masterpiece the world has known and embraced for generations and millennia. As it stands today - and I have seen it from a small screen in a beautiful little town in Greece to the largest Imax theatre in New York - it is a vastly overrated distraction from the real world, lacking the insight into that world's fragility that a masterpiece like Theo Angelopoulos's Ulysses' Gaze leads us to consider and contemplate.
