Pakistan's first lunar rover named 'Jinnah-1': Suparco. Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco) on Thursday announced “Jinnah-1” as the official name of the country’s first lunar rover. The rover is scheduled to be sent to the Moon in 2029 as part of China’s Chang’e-8 mission, where it will conduct scientific research at the lunar south pole, Suparco said. The Moon’s south pole is known for its challenging terrain and potential to yield significant scientific discoveries. In a ceremony held in Islamabad, Suparco said that the name was selected from 4,000 proposals received in a countrywide competition. Seven participants had proposed the name “Jinnah-1” and the winner was selected through a lucky draw, according to a statement from Suparco. Tayyab Karim, a 17-year-old from Bahawalnagar, was declared the winner for proposing the name, Suparco said. The name pays tribute to Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah and symbolises “Pakistan’s resolve, progress and new space horizons”, Suparco Chairman said. Jinnah-1 will study plasma, radiation and the lunar surface’s geology, as well as conduct key experiments related to future lunar research and the prospect of human presence on the Moon, Suparco said. Pakistan’s first lunar rover, Jinnah-1, will be a part of China’s Chang’e-8 mission to the Moon’s south pole in 2029. —Photo courtesy of Suparco Suparco announced the collaboration with China’s Chang’e-8 mission in 2024. “This collaboration marks a significant milestone for Pakistan’s space programme, as Suparco’s indigenous rover will be part of the mission to explore the lunar surface,” the space agency said at the time. Nasa is targeting 2028 for the first-ever landing of astronauts on the Moon’s south pole, as part of Artemis IV, seeking to beat China’s planned crewed mission, Chang’e-8, to the same lunar region. In 2023, India managed to land a craft — the unmanned Chandrayaan-3 — near the Moon’s south pole. Its landing came days after a Russian probe crashed in the same region and four years since the previous Indian attempt failed at the last moment.

Dar orders intensified diplomatic engagement for release of Pakistani sailors held hostage by Somali pirates. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar directed “stakeholders” on Thursday to maintain close and regular coordination and intensify diplomatic engagement with national and international partners to facilitate the release of 10 Pakistani sailors who have been held hostage by Somali pirates since April. The sailors were among the crew of the MT Honour 25, a Palau-flagged oil tanker that was hijacked by armed pirates off the coast of Puntland, Somalia, on April 21. Besides the 10 Pakistani crew members, the hostages also include seven Indonesians, including the captain, as well as an Indian and a Sri Lankan. During more than three months of their captivity, there has been no progress either in negotiations or the payment of the ransom, said to be around $3 million, for their recovery. Meanwhile, the Foreign Office (FO) has been saying that efforts continue for their release and return. In a statement posted on X today, it said Dar chaired a high-level meeting to review Pakistan’s “intensified efforts” for the safe release of the sailors. “The DPM/FM directed all relevant stakeholders to maintain close and regular coordination and intensify diplomatic engagement with national and international partners, including the Somali authorities and relevant international organisations, to facilitate the safe release of our citizens,” the FO stated. The FO said the government remained “fully seized” of the situation and that Dar expressed hope that sustained and coordinated engagement would lead to a positive outcome and the seamen’s safe return. It added that DPM Dar also expressed solidarity with the families of the sailors. On August 7, more than 100 days after being taken hostage by Somali pirates, the crew members on board MT Honour 25 released another distress message in which they had appealed directly to the Pakistani government for their release. In the two video messages, the Pakistani hostages and foreigners could be seen in a state of extreme distress, with most looking sick and weak. They requested that the Pakistani government talk to the Somali pirates and take steps to release them. Since the hijacking, the crew has made several emotional videos and audio appeals , while reporting that they have run out of clean water, food and medicine. The hostages are victims of an “ ownership crisis ”, as it is not clearly established who owns the ship and the man previously thought to be the owner was later revealed to be more likely a middleman who hired them. Earlier, under the supervision of the Somali pirates, there were several videos and phone calls to the families of the hostages to pressure them to pay the ransom. But after mid-June, the messages had stopped, until the latest appeal.

Air India mandates drug tests for all pilots after mid-air plunge. Air India pilots will undergo mandatory drug screening starting Thursday, according to an internal memo seen by AFP , after a captain involved in a serious mid-air incident reportedly tested positive for marijuana. Existing rules require airlines to randomly test at least 10 per cent of their flight crew for psychoactive substances each year. “We have decided to undertake a full screening of all Group pilots for any substances or medications that are not permitted under prevailing regulations,” the memo said. “Testing is mandatory and will start today.” On August 4, at least 24 passengers were injured when an Airbus A320 lost about 300 feet (91 metres) of altitude shortly after departing from Thailand’s Phuket for New Delhi. Local media reports said the main pilot had smoked marijuana and had tested positive in a second confirmatory test. Air India said the results have not been shared with them. Indian investigators have not commented on the reports but said they were closely examining evidence linked to the flight. The inquiry is being supported by Airbus and France’s civil aviation safety agency, the BEA. The incident came as Air India is seeking to overhaul its operations following a string of setbacks. Its reputation suffered a major blow in June 2025 when the London-bound Flight 171 crashed shortly after take-off from Ahmedabad, killing all but one of the 242 people on board and 19 people on the ground. Last week, the airline appointed former Ethiopian Airlines chief Tewolde Gebremariam as its new chief executive.

Karachi court acquits drug baroness Anmol ‘Pinky’ in 3 cases. KARACHI: A sessions court on Thursday acquitted alleged drug baroness Anmol alias Pinky in three narcotics cases registered at Karachi’s Gizri police station. The three cases were registered against Pinky at the Gizri police station in 2020, 2021 and 2022, and she had been declared an absconder. Additional District and Sessions Judge South Irshad Hussain heard Pinky’s pleas seeking acquittal. During the hearing, her counsel contended that she had been named in the cases on the basis of statements made by the co-accused, who had subsequently been acquitted. “Following the acquittal of the co-accused, there can be no case for conviction for the accused (Pinky),” the lawyer said. According to one of the court orders, a copy of which is available with Dawn , Pinky was named in a 2021 case by two accused arrested for possessing narcotics, who claimed that she had supplied the drugs to them. A supplementary charge sheet submitted by the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) last month revealed that Pinky had over a dozen cases registered against her. Anmol was arrested in May in connection with two cases registered at the Garden police station pertaining to the possession of drugs and an unlicensed weapon. She had already been booked in multiple other criminal cases prior to her arrest. The incident gained attention when a video of her being escorted to court without handcuffs went viral on social media. Since her arrest, Anmol has been presented in court amid heavy police presence. During her court appearances, she has also alleged that she has been facing pressure from the police “to take names ” of politicians and other influential persons.

China’s homegrown narrow-body jetliner completes second-ever international commercial flight. China’s homegrown C919 jetliner completed its second international commercial flight on Thursday, landing in Mongolia’s capital, Ulaanbaatar, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24. Flightradar24 earlier reported that the Air China flight was en route from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar, having departed at 3:36pm local time (12:36pm PKT). Tracking data later showed that the flight landed at 5:17pm local time (2:17pm PKT), completing the journey in one hour and 41 minutes. Flightradar24 noted that the C919 is scheduled to replace the 737 MAX on the route over the coming week. The narrow-body Comac C919 completed its first scheduled international commercial passenger flight on Wednesday, marking a milestone for the aircraft following its maiden commercial flight on May 28, 2023, according to Chinese news agency Xinhua . The flight from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar landed safely after one hour and 42 minutes and was welcomed with a water-salute ceremony at the airport. “The operation of this flight on the China-Mongolia international route demonstrates that the C919 has successfully passed the verification of bilateral international civil aviation operating standards, thereby officially acquiring the qualification for regular international commercial passenger operations,” Xinhua reported. It cited analysts as saying that the milestone flight marked a “starting point” for China’s domestically developed large passenger aircraft to gain global recognition. Tian Linchuan, an assistant researcher at the School of Aeronautics and Astronautics at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, said the ability to operate cross-border scheduled flights reliably demonstrated that “the C919 has reached the advanced level of its international counterparts in terms of safety, reliability and cost-effectiveness”, the agency reported. According to Xinhua , the C919 is China’s first self-developed trunk jetliner in accordance with international airworthiness standards and registered with independent intellectual property rights. It has already been successfully operating along multiple domestic routes since entering commercial service, gaining widespread market recognition due to its “reliable flight performance, comfortable cabin experience, and stable safety standards”, according to the agency. Air China currently operates 12 of these aircraft, and the C919 jet is also operated by China Eastern Airlines and China Southern Airlines, Xinhua added. The Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China, Ltd. (Comac), the developer of the jet, said that as of Aug 10 (Monday), the C919 had served 57 routes linking 25 cities and handled over 7.5 million passenger trips. The latest route between Beijing and Ulaanbaatar marks the 58th route and 26th linked city. Science and Technology Daily said that the steadily rising production capacity of C919 planes also supports their operation in overseas markets. Comac has set a target of reaching an annual production capacity of 200 aircraft by 2029, according to Xinhua.

NCCIA arrests 114 foreigners over alleged cyber-romance, sextortion network. ISLAMABAD: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has arrested 114 foreign nationals, including 111 Chinese and three Vietnamese citizens, for allegedly running a cyber-romance and sextortion network from a registered IT business in the capital. According to details released by the NCCIA’s media wing, the accused allegedly used electronic means and online platforms to target individuals in different countries. The network was allegedly involved in luring foreign nationals into online sexual conversations, including video chats and explicit video calls, and subsequently exploiting the material for criminal and financial purposes. Officials said the investigation also revealed indicators linking the accused to organised cybercrime activities, including cyber-romance-related financial fraud. NCCIA Islamabad has registered the case under Sections 14 and 21 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) 2016 , read with Sections 419, 420, 34 and 109 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) . Section 14 of Peca deals with electronic fraud. It criminalises using any information system, device or data to deceive a person for wrongful gain. It covers phishing, online scams and running fraudulent setups online. Offences under the section are punishable with up to two years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs10 million, or both. Section 21 deals with offences against the modesty of a natural person and a minor. It covers sexual blackmail, revenge porn, deepfakes and inducing a person to engage in sexually explicit acts online to cause harm, blackmail or extort them. It also provides for the immediate removal or blocking of such content by the NCCIA upon a complaint. Offences under the section are punishable with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs5 million. The punishment is more severe if the victim is a minor. Section 419 of the PPC deals with cheating by personation. It prescribes a punishment of up to seven years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both for impersonating another person to cheat. It also covers the use of fake profiles and identities on social media platforms. Section 420 of the PPC applies when a person is deceived into paying money or handing over property. It covers the financial fraud involved in cyber-romance scams, with the offence punishable by up to seven years’ imprisonment and a fine. Sections 34 and 109 of the PPC deal with common intention and abetment, respectively, and have been invoked to hold all members of the organised network liable, including planners, facilitators and financiers. The agency said further investigation was underway to establish the complete role of all those involved, identify additional victims and beneficiaries, and trace the financial and digital infrastructure used in the alleged activities. The NCCIA has also shared a list of the arrested individuals, along with their passport numbers.

Pakistan, Norway reaffirm resolve to strengthen bilateral ties, expand engagement in defence and security. Pakistan and Norway on Thursday reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral ties and expanding cooperation in defence and security. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, who is on a two-day visit to Pakistan, called on Chief of Defence Forces and the Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, with the two leaders reiterating their resolve to further strengthen bilateral ties and expand engagement in defence and security, according to a statement issued by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR). The two sides discussed matters of “mutual interest, regional security, and bilateral relations”. During the meeting, Field Marshal Munir highlighted “Pakistan’s perspective on global peace and regional stability” and stressed the “importance of cooperation and collaborative efforts to address common security challenges”. The Norwegian foreign minister appreciated the “professional role” played by the Pakistan Armed Forces “in promoting regional peace and stability”. Earlier in the day, Eide addressed a press conference alongside Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in Islamabad, during which he lauded Pakistan’s mediatory role in the US-Iran conflict, saying it was a “service to the world and hence, also to us”. “I also really want to reiterate our strong support for the very important role that Pakistan has taken in this dramatic war that started on February 28 with the US-Israel attack on Iran,” he said, recalling that Norway was one of the Western countries that was “clearest and earliest” in stating that the war was a violation of international rules. “If we stand up for international law, it has to apply to everyone, everywhere, all the time,” he stressed. He said that while Norway had “significant disagreements with Iran on other issues, they also have the right to be protected as a state”. Referring to Pakistan’s mediatory role in the ongoing conflict, he said he realised how difficult mediation and facilitation of parleys between the two sides could be. “I know what a massive task you were taking on when you offered Islamabad not only as the venue but also as the facilitator of these talks,” he said, lauding Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership for their efforts. “What you have been doing is really a service to the world, and hence, also to us.” The Norwegian diplomat said Pakistan’s mediation efforts also mattered to his country as it was a large shipping nation. “We share an interest in open sea lanes and the ability to trade in the high seas, and to respect the Constitution of the Oceans […] Whatever emerges from this tragic and unnecessary war in Gulf, we need to protect the principle of the free passage,” he explained. “And I am so happy we see completely eye to eye [on this],” he remarked. The visiting minister added that his message to “anyone involved out there in the conflict is that this issue of free passage and an open strait is not an issue for the warring parties alone. It is a global issue that we have a shared interest in promoting”. He said he had discussed other regional issues during the visit as well, ranging from the Kashmir issue to Afghanistan. Moreover, Eide said, he was glad to learn more about a recently signed defence pact between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia in Makkah. “These are three countries with whom Norway has very good and close relations,” he noted. At the outset of his address, Eide said he was honoured to be in Pakistan, saying the last time a Norwegian foreign minister visited Pakistan was 10 years ago. “So it was about time,” he remarked. “I promised you many months ago that I would come, and today, I live up to my promise. I was looking forward to this visit, which is short but very effective.” Eide said there was a “strong partnership” between Norway and Pakistan, as well as the people of the two countries. “We have a sizeable diaspora of Pakistani descent […] Many of them are in key positions of politics and society and are a very welcome contribution to our country; and the fact that we have so many people who know these two countries intimately is yet another argument for strengthening our economic ties,” he added. The Norwegian foreign minister further said that Oslo and Islamabad were discussing strengthening economic ties “in the context of specifics” and enhancing trade ties in more structural ways. He also mentioned climate change and floods in Pakistan, saying that the two sides agreed it was a foreign policy issue. “And if you need one additional argument for stopping wars apart from relieving suffering and ending economic harm, it is that mankind should collectively try to focus on the real issues that require real cooperative action,” he said. Eide said combating nature loss and climate change, promoting global health and fighting poverty were among the issues on his agenda for discussions during the visit. Speaking earlier, Dar said the two countries had agreed to enhance bilateral ties and cooperation in all areas of mutual interest, including trade and investment, education, defence, climate change, information technology and maritime affairs. He said Pakistan greatly valued its relations with Norway and looked forward to further strengthening them in the days, weeks and months ahead. Dar also said bilateral political consultations (BPC) between the two countries had become a regular feature of their engagement. “We are looking forward to hosting the next round of BPC in Islamabad later this year in the winter,” he said. Dar said the two sides also agreed that bilateral trade between Norway and Pakistan was “below the potential of both economies and needs to be enhanced through effective measures”. “Pakistan offers enormous investment opportunities to Norwegian companies, and it is heartening to see many leading Norwegian companies investing in Pakistan. “A renowned Norwegian company, Yara International, is establishing a joint venture in plant nutrition with the Fauji Fertiliser company. I hope this initiative will be a trailblazer for many more future projects between our two great countries,” he added. Dar termed Pakistan’s partnership with Norway in the field of technology “a success story”. “Pakistan’s IT exports to Norway have grown more than five-fold in the last two years, and I have no doubt that this is only the beginning.” He further stated that the two sides also agreed on the expedient finalisation of various agreements and memoranda of understanding (MoU). On climate change, he said there was a convergence of perspectives between the two countries. “It is heartening to note that Pakistan and Norway signed the MoU under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement on April 1 this year,” he said, adding that the two sides also held talks on cooperation in maritime affairs. He said he had told the visiting dignitary that Pakistan was “one of the world’s largest ship recycling facilities, and our strategic location makes it the most competitive and nearest recycling destination in this maritime region for ships coming from Norway”. Dar thanked Norway’s maritime authorities for their support in capacity building and providing technical training for Pakistan’s shipbreaking industry in line with the Hong Kong International Convention. He added that Pakistan and Norway had agreed to enhance people-to-people contact, which he said could become “defining for our relations and serve as social and cultural bridges between the two countries”. The DPM said the two sides had also discussed labour mobility. “We agreed to continue work on legal pathways for Pakistan’s skilled manpower, expressing the need to combat human smuggling and illegal migration. Both sides agreed that by providing safe, orderly and regular migration channels, we not only protect migrants’ rights and lives but also dismantle the illegal model of smuggling networks,” he elaborated. Dar further said that both Pakistan and Norway shared a commitment to multilateralism, the principles of the United Nations Charter, respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity and the peaceful settlement of disputes. “Our two countries remain actively engaged on issues related to the UN Security Council, and the two sides have strong convergence of views on major issues. “Building on our previous experience of working together in international bodies and multilateral fora, both sides affirm their desire to continue mutual support and consultations on such forums.” Dar said he had also briefed the Norwegian foreign minister and delegation on the Kashmir issue. He said he told them that India had added a new dimension to an already volatile security situation by unilaterally announcing the abeyance of the Indus Waters Treaty in contravention of international law. “We reiterate that India must end the weaponisation of water and uphold its treaty obligations under international legal obligations,” he asserted. Dar said he had further briefed the Norwegian foreign minister on Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts for promoting dialogue, de-escalation and peaceful settlement of the US-Iran conflict. He thanked him for appreciating Pakistan’s role as a mediator in the conflict. Moreover, he said, he had broadly discussed the Makkah defence pact with the visiting dignitary. “We had a great discussion, and it happens that all three countries enjoy the best of relations with Norway,” he said. The DPM concluded his address, saying: “We agreed on the need to find peaceful solutions to the international conflicts in full respect of the principles of international law and the UN Charter. “I thank his excellency, my dear friend, for his visit. I am confident that this visit will open a new chapter in Pakistan-Norway relations and will contribute to greater cooperation and mutual prosperity for the people of both countries in the years ahead.” Delegation-level talks Earlier in the day, Eide held delegation-level talks with DPM Dar, according to the Foreign Office (FO). During the talks, the two sides reviewed the whole gamut of bilateral cooperation in various fields, including trade, investment, climate change, maritime affairs and education. They recognised the important role of the Pakistani diaspora in Norway and agreed to strengthen people-to-people ties between the two countries. The two sides expressed satisfaction at the warm and cordial state of Pakistan-Norway relations and agreed to further deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest,” it said. FO said the two sides also held in-depth discussions on regional and international developments of mutual interest. During the delegation-level talks, the visiting dignitary also recognised Pakistan’s role in the US-Iran war as “important and constructive”, lauding the leadership of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Munir and DPM Dar, as per the FO statement. Eide had also appreciated Pakistan’s efforts to promote peace and expressed Norway’s desire to further strengthen bilateral ties earlier in the day in televised remarks. He said Norway and Pakistan had a “very strong bilateral partnership”, adding that the presence of a large Pakistani community in Norway, which was “well integrated into Norwegian society”, had helped strengthen ties between the two countries. “There are many leading politicians in Norway and many close colleagues who are actually of Pakistani-Norwegian descent, so it has really made a mark,” he said. Eide said business ties between the two countries were also growing, particularly in the energy and fertiliser sectors, with Norwegian companies increasingly looking at opportunities in Pakistan. He said Norway also saw opportunities for Pakistan to strengthen economic relations through its cooperation with Switzerland and Iceland, noting that the three countries could provide further avenues for expanding business relations. Turning to the regional situation, Eide strongly commended the actions taken by Pakistan’s leadership. Eide described the ongoing war as “incredibly dangerous” for global peace as well as the world economy, and praised Pakistan for stepping forward. He also appreciated Pakistan’s role in facilitating the Islamabad talks and maintaining engagement with the parties involved. “I think it is fair to say that the position of Pakistan on the world stage, also in peacemaking, has really been strengthened by this commitment,” he said. Eide said Norway was ready to assist Pakistan’s peace efforts, noting that Oslo had experience in peace negotiations and maintained open dialogue with both Tehran and Washington. “Wherever we can be useful, we will,” he said. He also highlighted Norway’s experience in international maritime affairs, saying the country was among the world’s major seafaring nations despite its relatively small population. He said Norway could therefore play a constructive role in discussions concerning international maritime law and developments surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Dar, Eide discuss bilateral ties The two ministers also held a “restricted-format meeting” earlier today, FO said. “DPM Dar warmly welcomed Eide to Pakistan. The two ministers discussed the full range of bilateral relations, as well as regional and international developments, and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation in all areas of mutual interest,” according to FO. Upon his arrival in Islamabad, Eide was received at the airport by Additional Foreign Secretary (Europe) Ambassador Ayesha Ali. In a statement on Wednesday, the FO said the minister is undertaking the visit from Aug 13-14 at Dar’s invitation. The visit is the first by a Norwegian foreign minister in a decade, the FO said, adding that the visit would build on high-level engagement between the two countries, including phone conversation between Dar and Eide in March and April , and the visit of Norway’s State Secretary Andreas Motzfeldt Kravik to Islamabad in May. The FO stated that the visit would provide an opportunity to “further strengthen the longstanding and cordial relations between Pakistan and Norway and to explore new areas of mutually beneficial cooperation”.

LHC issues judgement in 8-year-long public litigation, reaffirms environmental directions. LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Thursday issued its final judgment in an eight-year-old public interest litigation concerning smog and environmental degradation in Punjab, reaffirming its directions and achievements during the marathon proceedings. Justice Shahid Karim, who authored the judgment, described it as the “last judgment in the trilogy”, following two earlier reported rulings in 2023 and 2025 arising from the same continuing proceedings. Justice Karim, who is due to reach superannuation on August 19, began his judgment with a line from the final song in the play Hamilton : “Legacy, what is a legacy? It’s planting seeds in a garden you never get to see. I wrote some notes at the beginning of a song someone will sing for me.” The judge noted that the judgment culminated the extraordinary and seminal work accomplished in a novel and paradigmatic manner through the judicial review of public actions. “It does not mean that the goal has been accomplished. Far from it. Yet it sets the tone for future actions and lays the groundwork for building resilience and adaptation policies,” he added. He said that, during the course of the proceedings, governments had come on board, though reluctantly at times, and pursued policies based on the court’s decisions. He observed: “A robust culture of decision-making has developed with environmental and water conservation at its heart.” Justice Karim held that there had been critical questioning of the court’s authority to continue the proceedings unabated for more than eight years. “The short answer is the highly consequential issues animating and forming the core of this litigation,” he explained. Key directions and their compliance reaffirmed and consolidated in the judgment included: Smog as a calamity: On the court’s directions, smog was formally declared a calamity, with the Punjab Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) tasked with leading a dedicated control room for enforcement during the smog season. Brick kilns: Every operational brick kiln in Punjab has been converted to Zig-Zag Technology to cut emissions and each kiln has been assigned a Unique Identification Number for digital monitoring by the Environment Protection Agency. Stubble burning: The court raised penalties for stubble burning violations to Rs200,000 per acre after finding some districts were imposing fines as low as Rs50,000, and directed uniform enforcement across all Deputy Commissioners’ offices. School transport: Private schools have been directed to arrange buses or vans for at least 50 per cent of their students as a condition for registration renewal, to be implemented in phases. Water conservation: Amendments were made to LDA Building and Zoning Regulations making rainwater harvesting mandatory for new construction, and Gray Water Treatment Plants compulsory for all new commercial and residential building plans, with no building approvals to be granted without compliance. As many as 563 service stations across Lahore now operate water recycling plants, cutting fresh water use per car wash by roughly 70pc (from 400 litres to about 120 litres). Ablution water recycling tanks have been installed at over 194 mosques, including a 60,000–70,000-gallon facility at Data Darbar. Groundwater conservation: In compliance with the court’s orders, Wasa Lahore has collected over Rs3.35 billion in aquifer charges from bulk groundwater users since 2018. Separately, 117 recharge wells have been installed across Lahore, while rainwater storage tanks — including a 4-million-gallon facility at Gaddafi Stadium — have been built to combat flooding and recharge aquifers. Protection of public green spaces: The court barred playgrounds and open spaces — including at institutions such as MAO College — from being used for weddings or commercial events, and directed authorities, including DHA, LDA, and the School Education Department to protect and maintain green cover. Judicial review of development projects: The judgment also references two related rulings — the 2023 quashing of the Lahore Division Master Plan 2050 for violating LDA Master Plan Rules, and the striking down of land acquisition for a Gujrat Divisional Complex that would have required felling over 594 kanals of forest land — both cited as major environmental victories achieved through the same broader litigation. In his concluding remarks, Justice Karim paid tribute to the Judicial Water and Environment Commission’s members — retired Justice Ali Akbar Qureshi, Syed Kamal Ali Haider, Hina Hafeezullah Ishaq, and Ch. Zulfiqar Ali — who served pro bono throughout the proceedings. The judge recommended that they and several government officers involved in the implementation of the court’s directions be considered for civil awards. The judge disposed of the main petition filed by Haroon Farooq in 2018, along with a dozen petitions subsequently filed before the court concerning water and environmental issues. Justice Karim concluded the judgment with a poem by Amanda Gorman: “Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is time, that even as we grieved, we grew, that even as we hurt, we hoped, that even as we tired, we tried.”

Rabiul Awwal moon not sighted, Eid Miladun Nabi to fall on Aug 26. The Rabiul Awwal moon was not sighted, and Eid-i-Miladun Nabi will fall on August 26, Central Ruet-i-Hilal Committee Chairman Maulana Abdul Khabeer Azad announced on Thursday. The announcement was made following a meeting of the committee in Islamabad, while a notification issued by the Ministry of Religious Affairs stated that the first of Rabiul Awwal, 1448 AH, would commence on August 15 (Saturday). Representatives from the Pakistan Meteorological Department, the Ministry of Science and Technology and other relevant institutions provided technical support. Muslims around the world celebrate the birth of Prophet Muhammad (Peace Be Upon Him), known in Arabic as the Mawlid al-Nabawi holiday, on the 12th of Rabiul Awwal — the third month of the Islamic lunar calendar. On Saturday, Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah directed authorities to ensure foolproof security and uninterrupted civic facilities across the province for processions and religious gatherings on the day. Chairing a meeting with scholars from various schools of thought and senior officials, he said that it was the collective responsibility of the government to facilitate devotees in observing the sacred occasion in a peaceful, secure and clean environment. The chief minister directed the police, Rangers and district administrations to implement a coordinated security plan, ensure continuous monitoring and make effective deployments for all processions and Milad gatherings. The CM also instructed K-Electric, SSGC, the Karachi Water & Sewerage Corporation and other utility providers to ensure uninterrupted supplies of electricity, gas and water in areas around mosques, imambargahs and along procession routes.

Pakistan Army major general appointed new force commander of UN mission in Western Sahara. Pakistan Army Major General Jawwad Ahmed Qazi has been appointed the new force commander of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso), the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the UN announced on Thursday. In a social media post on X, Pakistan’s mission said, “UN Secretary General António Guterres has appointed Major Gen Qazi of Pakistan as the new force commander of Minurso.” “With over 35 years of leadership and operational experience in the Pakistan Army and UN peacekeeping, Major Gen Qazi brings extensive command, field and international experience to the mission,” the mission said. According to Pakistan’s mission, Major Gen Qazi has previously served in senior leadership roles, including command, staff and instructional positions, both in Pakistan and abroad. His previous appointments in Pakistan include general officer commanding of an infantry division, force commander in the Northern Areas and director general at the Ministry of Defence, it added. Earlier in his career, he also served with the UN Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Sirmium (UNTAES) in Croatia. “Pakistan takes pride in this appointment and remains committed to supporting UN peacekeeping and international efforts for peace and stability through deployment of mission-ready contingents and leaders who have vast peacekeeping experience,” it stated. Western Sahara, a former Spanish colony largely controlled by Morocco, is the only territory on the African continent whose post-colonial status has not been settled. Morocco has long been in conflict with the Algerian-backed Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the Sahrawi people. It is claimed by the Polisario Front, which insists on the indigenous Sahrawi people’s right to a referendum on self-determination monitored by the UN. Polisario is seeking independence and says Morocco should adhere to an agreement it accepted in 1991 that provides for a UN-supervised referendum on self-determination.

Yadgar-i-Fatah monument inaugurated in Islamabad on eve of Independence Day. The Yadgar-i-Fatah monument, built to honour Pakistan’s martyrs and commemorate Marka-i-Haq , was inaugurated by President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad on Thursday night, on the eve of the country’s 80th Independence Day. President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmad Babar Sidhu and Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf were in attendance and stood for the national anthem, played by a military band. Foreign diplomats, military attaches, officers of the three services and other senior officials were also in attendance. (From L-R) Chief of Air Staff Air Marshal Zaheer Ahmad Babar Sidhu, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attend the inauguration ceremony of the Yadgar-i-Fatah monument in Islamabad on August 13, 2026. — Screengrab via YouTube/ISPR Official ‘Guarantor of peace’ Addressing the ceremony, Prime Minister Shehbaz congratulated the nation on Independence Day and said that under Quaid-i-Azam’s leadership, “we entered the realm of freedom from the darkness of slavery. Our elders sacrificed their lives and property”. “Yadgar-i-Fatah symbolises our resolve and determination and the domination of our armed forces over the enemy,” he added. The premier also congratulated the nation on Marka-i-Haq and paid tribute to Field Marshal Munir for his leadership during the conflict, as well as Air Chief Marshal Sidhu and Admiral Ashraf. “Under his leadership, we defeated the enemy,” PM Shehbaz said. Paying tribute to the architects and engineers who designed the monument, the premier expressed appreciation for its sleek design and eight-month completion time. “Its completion in eight months would not have been possible if the field marshal hadn’t invested his deep interest,” PM Shehbaz added. “This is not just a monument of blocks, but a tribute to the martyrs who sacrificed their lives to defend the nation. That triumph is the victory of our army and our people, and this is our pride.” He noted that Pakistan wants peace, not war, and that desiring peace should not be perceived as a sign of weakness. “With dignity and determination, we are resolute for peace,” the premier stated, adding that Pakistan had been recognised as a “guarantor of peace” in the region. “If anyone challenges Pakistan’s sovereignty and defence, they will receive an even stronger reply than in May 2025,” he warned. PM Shehbaz noted that after suffering defeat, India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty unilaterally. “I warn that every drop of water is our red line. If India does not keep on the right track, we will give it a direct response,” he further warned. Speaking about the future of the country, PM Shehbaz recognised that doors needed to be opened for the younger generation. “We need to incorporate the latest technology to advance in the journey of our economic progress. We need to develop our human resources so our country will enter into a new phase of progress and well-being,” he stressed. “We must make a Pakistan where all provinces, including Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir, will advance and develop together.” A world free of conflict The premier added that the nation wants to see a world “free from all sorts of conflict”. “We want to resolve all the issues with justice and in accordance with the UN Charter,” he emphasised, highlighting Islamabad’s role as a mediator between Iran and the US in the ongoing Middle East War. “The Makkah Agreement is the promise of peace for the Middle East, and a hope of peace for the Muslim world. It is also a message of peace for the whole world,” PM Shehbaz added. He further stated that Pakistan would keep advocating for the oppressed Palestinians and supporting their right to self-determination, while adding that Islamabad wants peace in Afghanistan, but the use of its soil for cross-border terrorism was “unacceptable”. “We need to stay united for peace and development. We need to bury the hate and revive the love for each other by forgetting our differences,” he emphasised. ‘We are not a small country to play with’ Taking the podium, President Zardari said that the nation and its armed forces, under Field Marshal Munir’s dynamic leadership, gave a befitting answer to India during the war last year. “This is in faith to remember what happened, in how many days it happened, where it happened, and this will go down in history for everyone to remember, whether today or the day after,” he said. He noted that Pakistan’s military response to Indian aggression demonstrated that “we are not a small country for you to play with”. “We are there as partners to the world, in the … family of countries,” President Zardari added. “And I think, today, even they understand that Pakistan is a national partner.” He added that the monument reflects the unity of the nation, the strength of the armed forces and the sacrifices given. The president recalled that his own father was called upon by Quaid-i-Azam to fight in the 1948 Kashmir War. “Most of Sindh, KP, other places, anybody who could carry an arm were there, and they fought against the Indian Army,” he stated. “By the grace of God, we got our Durand Line, our border line, but still so, a lot needs to be done … by us, the people and the public and definitely, the coming generation of Pakistan.” President Zardari noted that the premier, the CDF, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi were playing a “most commendable and praiseworthy” role. “We’ve been successful till now. Life comes and goes … we’ve seen tragedies, we’ve seen successes [and] successfully managed to guide our system through,” he added. “I’m not saying there would not be weaknesses; there always are; but there is no nation in the world that can claim they have no weaknesses.” Prior to the speeches by the country’s leadership, visuals broadcast on television showed a large contingent of personnel from the military, paramilitary forces and police presenting a guard of honour, accompanied by a military band. Personnel from the military, paramilitary forces and police present their standards during the inauguration ceremony of the Yadgar-i-Fatah monument in Islamabad on August 13, 2026. — Screengrab via YouTube/ISPR Official Yadgar-i-Fatah monument The marble monument was completed within eight months and features five archways, which represent the five pillars of Islam, as well as the five pillars of Pakistan itself — the government, the military, the media, the people and the ideology underpinning the nation. Additionally, they represent the three branches of the military — the Army, the Air Force and the Navy — as well as cyber-defence and space warfare. As part of the inauguration, a light and sound show was presented with moving images projected directly onto the monument, state television showed. One of the sequences highlighted the history of Pakistan and its military up until Marka-i-Haq . Iconic moments from the May war were also projected onto the monument, such as when villagers and Punjab Rangers shot at Indian drones together. Moving graphics are directly projected onto the Yadgar-i-Fatah monument during its inauguration ceremony in Islamabad on August 13, 2026. — Screengrab via YouTube/PTV News Following the light show, Pakistan Air Force fighter jets performed a flypast over the monument, deploying flares in the night sky. A Pakistan Air Force fighter jet performs a flypast over the Yadgar-i-Fatah monument in Islamabad on August 13, 2026. — Screengrab via YouTube/PTV News The monument marks Pakistan’s victory over India in a brief military conflict last May. The conflict with India — starting from the April 22 Pahalgam attack to the end of Operation Bunyanum Marsoos with a ceasefire between the two countries on May 10 — has been called “ Marka-i-Haq ” (Battle of Truth) by the state.

SC judges’ pay, benefits raised to FCC-level. • Judges’ salaries raised to Rs1.5m per month • Afridi to remain ‘CJP’ until retirement, title will subsequently go to whoever is senior among FCC and SC chief justices ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zar­dari has approved an increase in the salaries, judicial allowance and pension benefits of Supreme Court judges, bringing them at par with those of judges of the newly constituted Federal Constitu­tional Court (FCC), effective from Dec 10, 2025. Under the Salary of Judges of the Supreme Court Order, 2026, the monthly salary of Supreme Court judges has been increased to Rs1.5 million from the earlier Rs1.16m. The order will come into force immediately and will be deemed to have taken effect from Dec 10, 2025. However, Chief Justice Yahya Afridi will receive a monthly salary of Rs1.6m, although the order specifies Rs1.55 million as the salary of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Justice Yahya Afridi will receive the enhanced salary of Rs1.6m as he has been designated as the Chief Justice of Pakistan (CJP). He will also retain the coveted title of CJP until his superannuation on Oct 26, 2027, following a last-minute change introduced through the 27th Constitution Amendment. Earlier, it was believed that the title would eventually go to the chief justice of the FCC. The substitution made in Clause 23 of Article 176 clarifies that the incumbent Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, who is Justice Yahya Afridi, will continue to hold the title of CJP for the remainder of his term. Justice Afridi was sworn in as the 30th Chief Justice of Pakistan in October 2024, for a three-year term. Another provision introduced through the amendment defines the CJP, after the retirement of the incumbent, as the senior of the two chief justices — that is, the chief justices of the FCC and the Supreme Court. This provision will come into effect after the retirement of the incumbent CJP. The issue was further clarified when Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar rejected the impression that the 27th Amendment had abolished the office of the CJP. Speaking on the floor of the National Assembly, the law minister said the office had not been abolished and that CJP Afridi would continue to head key judicial bodies, including the Supreme Judicial Council (SJC) and the Judicial Commission of Pakistan. After his retirement, however, the position of CJP will go to whichever of the two chief justices — of the FCC or the Supreme Court — is senior. To increase the salary of the CJP, the president also approved the Chief Justice of Pakistan Order, 2026, which will be deemed to have taken effect from July 1, 2026. Likewise, under the Supreme Court Judges (Leave, Pension and Privileges) (Amendment) Order, 2026, which will also take effect from Dec 10, 2025, an amendment has been made to paragraph 22, under which a judge will be entitled to a monthly superior judicial allowance of Rs1.5m. Similarly, an amendment to paragraph 16 provides that the pension of the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court will be calculated at 85pc and 75pc, respectively, of the salary as determined by the president. In addition, paragraph 19 has been amended by inserting a provision under which a judge will be entitled to a monthly medical allowance of Rs150,000. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

Punjab govt launches ‘paperless governance’. LAHORE: Punjab goes paperless as Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz on Thursday launched “government-to-government, government-to-business and government-to-citizen” services. The CM said the Punjab government had become the first province to establish e-FOAS, e-Procurement, e-Pay, e-Auction, OneMap, HRMIS and a data warehouse. She presided over an online meeting to review the progress in digitalisation and the automation. Chairman Punjab Information Technology Board (PITB) Faisal Yousaf briefed the participants. The CM directed the PITB to take steps for importing paperless automation software and ordered continuous feedback from applicants. She said that an end-to-end automated paperless system would prove effective in eliminating corruption. “We want to save people from the inconvenience of visiting government offices for even minor tasks.” Ms Nawaz said services provided through a digital automation system without requiring applicants to reveal their identity would help eliminate corrupt elements. “We are putting every sector, every department and every institution of Punjab on the path to digitalisation,” she declared and added that the entire team was working as one unit for digitalisation and automation. She said automation services system eliminated the need for interaction with government officials, thereby ensuring transparency. The meeting was informed that more than 6,000 systems had been connected with the PITB’s central system in the province, while 600 organisations and institutions had been digitally connected through e-FOAS. The e-filing system had issued 176,173 summary notices and resulted in savings of Rs9.1m. The briefing further revealed that smart monitoring of development projects had established a new benchmark for transparency in development schemes. More than 25,000 suppliers had been connected with the province-wide e-procurement system, under which digital purchases worth Rs6tr and 1.29m tenders had been processed. “The e-Procurement system had introduced a transparent, end-to-end tendering mechanism without requiring applicants to visit any government office, resulting in savings of Rs1.3 million. Revenue collection through transactions had reached Rs1.137bn,” the meeting was told. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

Petroleum levy collection hits record Rs1.57tr. • Cost of running civil govt rises 16pc, crosses Rs1tr for first time • Fiscal deficit shrinks to 2.6pc on the back of provincial surpluses, lower interest bill • Defence spending up 18pc; primary surplus reaches record 2.9pc of GDP ISLAMABAD: With a record Rs1.567 trillion petroleum levy collection amid record consumer-end oil prices following US-Israel attacks on Iran, the cost of running the civil government rose 16 per cent in the fiscal year 2025-26 to cross Rs1tr for the first time despite restructuring and austerity measures, official data showed on Thursday. At the same time, record cash surpluses from the provinces and a sharp fall in interest payments helped contain the fiscal deficit at 2.6pc of GDP — the lowest since FY03 for which comparable data is available on the Ministry of Finance website — while the primary surplus reached a historic 2.9pc of GDP. In its annual report on fiscal operations for FY26, the Ministry of Finance reported that petroleum levy collection surged 29pc to Rs1.567tr from Rs1.22tr a year earlier. It also surpassed the original budget target of Rs1.468tr, which had subsequently been revised upward to Rs1.498tr as part of the FY27 budget exercise. The Rs1.567tr petroleum levy did not include an undisclosed amount of customs duty and Rs26bn collected through the carbon levy. For the current fiscal year, the government is targeting an even higher Rs1.676tr in petroleum levy, besides Rs50bn through the climate levy on petroleum products. Despite restructuring and austerity policies, expenditure on running the civil government increased by 16pc to Rs1.033tr from Rs892bn in FY25, breaching the Rs1tr mark for the first time and exceeding the Rs971bn budget estimate. Defence expenditure also increased by 18pc to Rs2.588tr from Rs2.194tr a year earlier. How­ever, it was only Rs38bn higher than the Rs2.55tr budget allocation despite additional requirements following Indian attacks. Total revenue collection declined marginally to 15.6pc of GDP in FY26 from 15.7pc a year earlier. Federal Board of Revenue collection stood at Rs13.01tr, around 10pc short of target but almost 11pc higher than Rs11.74tr collected in FY25. Despite the revenue shortfall, historically high provincial cash surpluses and a steep decline in interest payments enabled the government to sharply reduce the overall fiscal deficit. The primary surplus — the difference between total revenues and expenditure excluding debt servicing — reached 2.9pc of GDP, the highest since the government began reporting the indicator in FY20. The fiscal deficit had peaked at 8.9pc of GDP in FY19 before falling to 8.1pc and 7.1pc in the following two years. It rose again to 7.9pc in FY22 but has since declined amid successive IMF-backed fiscal tightening. Meanwhile, the primary account remained in deficit until turning into a surplus of 0.9pc of GDP in FY24. It improved to 2.4pc the following year and further to 2.9pc in FY26. Three major contributors to the fiscal improvement were record provincial cash surpluses of Rs1.45tr, petroleum levy collection of Rs1.567tr and a Rs1.939tr decline in interest payments. The finance ministry reported that interest payments fell to Rs6.947tr, or 5.5pc of GDP, from Rs8.887tr, or 7.7pc of GDP, in FY2024-25 — a dec­line equivalent to 2.2pc of GDP in a single year. Subsidies were also contained at Rs1.01tr, almost 22pc below Rs1.3tr in FY25, while development expenditure fell to Rs727bn from Rs786bn. Mainly because of savings on interest payments following the easing of the policy rate from 22pc to 10pc, total expenditure declined to Rs23.09tr from Rs24.16tr in FY25. As a result, total expenditure fell to 18.2pc of GDP from 21.1pc a year earlier. Current expenditure also declined to 16.3pc of GDP (Rs20.69tr) from 18.8pc (Rs21.5tr) in FY25. Defence expenditure, however, edged up to 2pc of GDP from 1.9pc. The four provinces posted a 57pc increase in their combined cash surplus to the Centre, taking it to a record Rs1.45tr from Rs921bn in FY25 — an increase of Rs529bn in a single year. They had committed a surplus of Rs1.38tr under the national fiscal pact. Punjab alone provided Rs915bn — almost equivalent to the combined Rs921bn surplus of all four provinces a year earlier and 163pc higher than its Rs348bn contribution in FY25. Sindh followed with a 24pc increase in its surplus to Rs350bn from Rs283bn. PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provided Rs165bn, around 6pc lower than Rs176bn in FY25, while Balochistan posted a surplus of just Rs20.74bn. On the accounting side, the government reported a record statistical discrepancy of Rs853bn. The discrepancy stood at Rs329bn in FY25 and had drawn concern from the IMF, which had suggested a technical mission that the government declined. The finance ministry attributed Rs448bn of the discrepancy to under-reporting at the federal level and Rs405bn to provinces. It said the federal discrepancy stemmed from “variations on account of time lag in reporting and book adjustments amongst SBP, FBR and EAD data”. At the provincial level, Rs266bn of the discrepancy was attributed to increases in commercial bank deposits, while KP and Balochistan accou­nted for Rs95bn and Rs72bn, respectively, also largely due to movements in bank deposits. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

The unfinished independence. EVERY August, we raise the flag and call ourselves free. But on the first morning of that freedom, in 1947, Faiz, in Subh-i-Azadi , looked at the long-awaited dawn and said it was not the one: ‘yeh da agh daagh ujala, yeh shab-gazida sehar ’ — this stained, night-bitten dawn is not the morning we had set out for. Seventy-nine years on, our national day deserves an honest question: did we win a country and quietly postpone its freedom? In 1947, we changed the nationality of our rulers and left the harder task — changing the nature of rule — to a later generation. That is our unfinished independence — still ours to finish. Begin with the one thing the British empire left behind that no repeal can reach: not a law, but a habit of mind. Colonial rule does not merely occupy a land; it occupies the imagination of those it governs, teaching them to see themselves through the ruler’s eyes — as subjects to be managed, not citizens to be served; supplicants at a counter, not owners of the state. Ashis Nandy called colonialism, above all, a colonisation of the mind — a condition that outlives the flag. This servility was not an accident of empire; it was its design. In 1835, Lord Macaulay told the British that education in India should produce a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect — trained not to rule but to serve. That reflex — to defer, to request rather than require, to treat power as something that happens to us rather than something that belongs to us — is the empire’s most durable export. A new nation needs strong institutions to hold power to account — parties with roots, a parliament with nerve. We did not yet have them: our leadership was thin and soon thinned further, our parties young and quarrelsome. India inherited a mass movement decades in the making and gave itself a constitution within three years. We took nine — nine years without the rules of a shared game, which are exactly the years in which a political culture is meant to grow. Into that vacuum stepped the two institutions the empire had built to their fullest strength — the army and the civil service, disciplined and sure of themselves while everything else improvised. The old colonial master had sailed home; a new establishment, home-grown but colonial in instinct, took his chair. That is the quiet tragedy of our first independence: we did not defeat colonialism so much as change its address. How do we raise citizens — and judges — with the strength to say no when power sits across the table offering everything? And here I must speak of my own house, for the gravest damage was done not by generals or bureaucrats but by judges. The judiciary was meant to be the citizen’s shield — the one institution whose purpose is to say no to power on the authority of law. But it too was a colonial inheritance, and carried the reflex in its bones: under the Raj it had served the sovereign, not the subject, and at independence it transferred that loyalty from the departed Crown to the new establishment, not the people. So when the tanks rolled, the courts, again and again, said yes. They fashioned a doctrine of necessity to legalise the seizure of power; they swore in usurpers; they dressed lawlessness in the robes of law. The colonial mind inside the judiciary has cost this country more than any single dictator, for it turned the guardian of the Constitution into the notary of its breach. Why did they give in? For three human reasons that have nothing to do with law. The first is fear: independence has cost judges their careers, their liberty, at times their lives. The second, and the least confessed, is comfort — the office, the title, the house and the car. The third is isolation — the weight of standing alone when colleagues have already found reasons to look away. What resists them is the one thing a law degree does not issue: character. So the question for our second independence is disarmingly simple: how do we raise citizens — and judges — with the strength to say no when power sits across the table, speaking softly and offering everything? Here I have reached a conviction that may sound strange: that strength is not built by law. It is built by the humanities. History dismantles the oldest alibi of every surrender — the plea that ‘these times are unprecedented’ and so exempt from principle; whoever knows history has heard that lie before, and knows how it ends. Philosophy teaches us to reason about ends, not merely means. Literature is our only sustained practice at inhabiting another human being, without which justice is merely filing. That is why the second independence will begin not in a courtroom or a parliament but in a classroom. If we want judges who will not sign the unjust order, we must form them long before they reach the bench — students given not only the mechanics of the law but a settled conviction about what the Constitution is for. The student of conviction becomes the honest lawyer; the honest lawyer, the fearless bar leader; the fearless bar leader, the judge who says no. Give a generation that conviction and no amendment can take it from them, for a conviction cannot be amended. Pakistan was dreamed by a poet and argued into being by a lawyer — Iqbal’s conviction, Jinnah’s case. Somewhere we kept the lawyer and forgot the poet, and were left with arguments but no convictions. This Independence Day, let us call the poet back — into our schools, our courts, and our idea of what an educated citizen owes his country. The dawn Faiz described is still stained. He told us to keep walking — ‘ chale chalo ’ — for the true morning has not yet come. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He is currently the Distinguished Chair in Constitutionalism & Justice and Professor of Practice at the Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, Lums. Published in Dawn, August 14th, 2026

The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Coalition buys time on judges, but harder questions persist. WHILE it seems that the deadlock over judges’ appointments has been resolved for now, there are still many sticking points souring ties between the PML-N and PPP, which would have to be addressed in the days to come, Dawn has learnt. The bad blood from recriminations over the conduct of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir had hardly settled when the two ruling allies found themselves in a standoff over the appointment of high court judges, nominated by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP). The matter, which was finally resolved on Tuesday after being delayed for several weeks, is just one of the many bumps on the road for the two coalition partners, who have recently found themselves at odds over three major issues — AJK elections, the appointments of new judges, and the reopening of a debate on new provinces. In background discussions, leaders from both parties told Dawn that while the PPP is looking to their leadership for guidance on how to proceed under the circumstances, the PML-N may prefer to defer discussion on sensitive issues — especially the question of new provinces — for as long as possible, lest it derail the coalition’s ‘marital bliss’, so to speak. PPP insiders say party still mulling course of action; PML-N wants to leave ‘touchy subject’ of new provinces for next assembly to tackle On Monday night, a crucial meeting was held in Parliament House to settle the judges’ issue. In attendance was President Asif Ali Zar­dari’s legal team, including his legal adviser Irfan Qadir, Sindh Law Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar and Karachi Mayor Barrister Murtaza Wahab. Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, meanwhile, was the sole representative from the government’s side. Arranged by the National Assembly Secretariat, the meeting was held on a single-point agenda, i.e. the delayed notification of high court judges, a source privy to the meeting told Dawn. Earlier reports had indicated that the president’s legal team had objected to the JCP proceedings, noting that nearly all PPP nominees had been rejected, and that some of the recommended candidates even had criminal records. While the government had been considering the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to bypass the need for presidential approval of the decision, the option became less attractive after the Islamabad High Court took up the matter and issued notices to all parties concerned. With the matter becoming sub judice, both sides felt it was more prudent to settle the matter ‘out of court’, leading to Monday’s confab that finally broke the deadlock over the JCP-sanctioned appointments. A senior PPP office-bearer told Dawn that the meeting with the government and President Zardari’s subsequent assent for the judicial appointments were meant to avoid any adverse decision from the court. However, with around a couple of dozen judicial vacancies still to be filled, insiders say it is ext­remely likely that some PPP nominees will be accommodated in the next round of appointments. According to the PPP leader, the government side had assured the party that in the future, all major decisions will be taken after consultation. However, such promises have been made and broken in the past as well. Future of the coalition? When asked about the future of the coalition partnership, the leader said that barring some political skirmishes — which were par for the course — the alliance between the two parties would continue. However, the PPP office-bearer was adamant that his party would not defend any unconstitutional move, whether regarding the creation of new provinces, or any other issue. Talking to Dawn , another party leader from Karachi said that while the Presidency had broken the ice with the PML-N, party leaders are still waiting for guidance from Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on how to proceed. When asked about the thinking behind the Presidency’s relenting on the issue of judges, the party leader said that while Mr Zardari believed in the “politics of reconciliation” and was “always willing to give others some space”, his son’s stance is usually quite tough. “He does not settle for less,” the PPP leader said of Bilawal’s approach, adding: “That is why I am saying that the party’s direction on its relationship with the government will be determined by the chairman’s actions or statements, and not by the party’s response to any move initiated by the government”. Transporters’ issues almost resolved: Sindh CM. • Murad Ali Shah directs transport department to address remaining demands • KATI warns prolonged strike could disrupt production, essential supplies • LCCI calls for meaningful dialogue to end strike; says export containers worth $500 million stranded at factories KARACHI: As the goods transporters’ strike entered its sixth day on Thursday, continuing to disrupt industrial activity and exports, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah claimed that the dispute was “almost resolved” and only a few points remained under discussion. Govt remains committed to Balochistan’s flood-hit people. ISLAMABAD: The government remains committed to the rehabilitation of every eligible family affected by the devastating floods of 2022, the Ministry of Planning and Development has said. The commitment comes in the wake of reports that the provincial and federal governments had restructured a World Bank-funded flood rehabilitation project, depriving a large number of affected families in Balochistan of the resilient homes they were promised. In a statement, the planning ministry maintained that 68,992 fully damaged or destroyed houses in Balochistan were identified as eligible for reconstruction assistance by the Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA). Each one of them remains entitled to the housing assistance committed under the Integrated Flood Resilience and Adaptation Programme (IFRAP). In addition, the ministry said, the project provides self-recovery support for 58,016 partially damaged houses. Planning ministry says work has commenced on 74,988 houses, of which 26,357 have already been completed under owner-driven construction model According to the statement, as of August 10, construction had commenced on 74,988 houses, of which 26,357 had already been completed under the project’s owner-driven reconstruction model. The ministry maintained that since IFRAP was conceived as a multi-sectoral recovery and resilience programme, it does not simply mean rebuilding houses while leaving communities without schools, healthcare, irrigation, roads, water, livelihoods and protection against the next disaster. It said that the decision to redirect WB funding from one sector to another was taken by the project steering committee — led by Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal — and that the resources were allocated within Balochistan. “A family whose house has been rebuilt still needs a functioning school for its children, a health facility for its elderly and sick, irrigation water for its crops, a road to reach the market and opportunities for its young people to earn a livelihood,” the statement said. The statement said that housing is the only major IFRAP component financed above its originally authorised cost, with financing for housing standing at approximately $161 million against an approved PC-1 cost of $155m. The ministry, however, said that it takes concerns about project implementation and performance seriously, which is why the Project Steering Committee has already ordered an independent high-level inquiry. Its purpose is to establish the facts transparently, examine any shortcomings in implementation and fix responsibility wherever warranted. Our Staff Reporter adds: According to World Bank project documents and minutes of meetings, IFRAP’s dedicated Housing Reconstruction Unit identified 231,749 eligible beneficiaries, and provided additional financing in 2025 to increase the project funding to $161m to support a total of 97,000 eligible beneficiaries. It was the IFRAP project steering committee which decided that housing support may be capped at the 62,966 first-tranche beneficiaries approved as of June 22, 2026, while housing subsidy support would remain capped at 97,000. WB Country Director Bolormaa Amgaabazar noted in a July 30 letter that this decision leaves 119,049 verified and eligible households without financing support, and expressed concern that making this decision public means that households that completed verification and signed the project undertakings may continue to expect assistance. She highlighted that 66,120 exclusion-related grievances had already been registered in the project grievance management system on or before the agreed cut-off date and that such an exclusion could aggravate poverty situation in the provinces.
