Two-Nation Theory and genesis of Pakistan. IN South Asia, the rise of Muslim political consciousness and the creation of Pakistan reflected a prolonged constitutional and political struggle led by Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The demand for Pakistan was rooted in the belief that the Muslims of British India constituted a distinct political community whose cultural, religious, and political interests required constitutional protection and effective political representation. Pakistan’s national identity has consequently remained closely associated with the ideas that formed the raison d’être for the Pakistan Movement. Its history offers lessons that can be learnt from significant events, most notably the political crisis of 1971, which culminated in the separation of East Pakistan. The post-1971 period also witnessed continuing debates over the nature of the federation, provincial autonomy, and national identity. These debates underline the importance of learning from history rather than using it to promote narrow political narratives. Pakistan’s political experience demonstrates that national cohesion depends not only on shared historical ideals but also on constitutional governance, political inclusion, social justice, and respect for diversity. The enduring challenge, therefore, is to reconcile Pakistan’s historical foundations with the requirements of a modern, democratic, and inclusive state to dispel the spread of unsubstantiated narratives against the Two-Nation Theory as an ideological basis of Pakistan. Pakistan’s leadership must follow the Quaid’s democratic vision and understand the primacy of Jinnah’s thoughts in tackling constitutional, political, economic and security challenges. The dilemma that crystallised after the 1857 War of Independence was the result of wilful distortions and misconceptions about the Muslims of British India. The British believed that Muslims were the real ‘troublemakers’ responsible for the uprising. Their hostile attitude towards Muslims caused exploitation and generated feelings of deprivation among them. They lost social status and suffered cruel punishments. During this dark phase of the community’s life Sir Syed Ahmad Khan dispelled the idea that Muslims were responsible for the war. The Aligarh movement he launched was based on a trinity of ideas: loyalty to the British, distance from politics, and devotion to education. His educational movement started to bring lasting change in the outlook of Muslim community. In the beginning Sir Syed was in favour of Hindu-Muslim unity; he considered India as a bride and Hindus and Muslims as the two eyes of the bride. Nevertheless, in 1867, after the Hindi-Urdu controversy, he realised that both communities were separate. Thus, Muslims became aware of their own distinctive political identity in the subcontinent. They acted on the advice of Sir Syed and cooperated with the British. They did not join the Indian National Congress (INC), which was established in 1885 to provide a common platform for Indians and to introduce the concept of one nation. It was clear that the organisation based on Western type of democracy would not be able to protect Muslim interests due to dominance of Hindus. Crystallisation of Sir Syed’s thoughts formed the Two-Nation Theory. It was not only the religious and social aspect of life where there were divergences between the two communities. There were little or no common customs and traditions shared by both communities. The structure, function and shape of houses and places of worship belonging to both communities were different. The variance was much wider in cuisine. There were no common festivals and celebrations among Hindus and Muslims. The language spoken by Hindus and Muslims was Hindustani, used for the purpose of communication. However, for literary purposes Muslims used Urdu, which absorbed many Arabic, Persian and Turkish words. Hindus used Hindi as a source of literature, which consisted of high percentage of Sanskrit words. Thus, both languages expressed fundamentally different ideas and shared different cultural expressions. This difference went deeper in poetry. Urdu poetry expressed themes of loneliness, amazement, and depiction of Muslim life shared across many countries in a very different way using metaphors, abstraction, and philosophical manner compared to Hindi poetry, which depicted local environment and described emotions. Muslims realised that they had different outlook, beliefs, traditions, language, and inclinations. Their apprehension of losing their status and suppression of their identity motivated them to bring homogeneity to their nationhood under the prevailing claustrophobic social and political order. The Two-Nation Theory impelled its adherents to follow a joint line of action for the accomplishment of their goal. It shaped the ideological form of the Pakistan Movement and gave birth to a new nation. The Two-Nation Theory was a revolt against the prevailing exploitation of Muslims by the British and domination of Hindus in British India, where Hinduism was being imposed on Muslims and their culture. Based on the Two-Nation Theory Muslims demanded a separate electorate in 1906. The British, through the Minto-Morley reforms, allowed separate electorates by recognising Muslims as a separate nation. Achieving separate statutory status was a triumph and proved a hallmark in Indian politics. Through the Lucknow Pact of 1916, the Quaid tried to bring the two communities closer, and he was called the “ambassador of Hindu-Muslim unity”. It was a tremendous achievement of Jinnah that Congress also recognised Muslims as a separate nation. Jinnah worked towards the goal of uniting both communities until M.K. Gandhi started playing the communal card. Gandhi publicly said that “a body of converts cannot call themselves a nation.” In response to this the Quaid replied in a public statement that by all canons of international law, the Muslims constituted a nation. Quaid-i-Azam understood that the Indian Muslims could compete with the Congress only when they showed they could settle their own differences. Jinnah declared the Muslims to be a nation with its own “distinctive culture and civilisation, language and literature, art and architecture, names and nomenclature, sense of values and proportion, legal laws and moral codes, customs and calendar, history and tradition, aptitude and ambition.” The expression of the Two-Nation Theory was reflected in his famous 14 Points. This legal framework provided for effective representation of Muslims in all law-making bodies, protection of Muslim territories, their religious liberty, culture, language, education, personal laws, customs, and their religious institutions. The movement for the partition of India gained strength when the poet-philosopher Allama Dr Muhammad Iqbal conceived the geographical shape of a homeland for Muslims. During his address in 1930 at Allahabad, Allama Iqbal said: “I would like to see the Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan amalgamated into a single state. Self-government within the British Empire, or the formation of a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim state, appears to me to be the final destiny of the Muslims at least of North-West India.” The Quaid’s return from England to India in 1934 marked a turning point in politics. He was convinced that constitutional safeguards alone might not secure the political future of India’s Muslims, and began to articulate a more determined vision of separate homeland for Muslims by converting Iqbal’s dream into reality. The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy, expanded the electorate, and established provincial legislatures. Despite reservations, both the Congress and the Muslim League contested the 1937 elections. Congress emerged victorious in several provinces and formed ministries, including in areas with Muslim majority. The Congress rule proved politically devastating for Muslims. The Congress ministries promoted Hindu culture and policies at the expense of Muslim identity. The Wardha education scheme became a particular source of controversy. Congress, for revival of Hinduism, introduced Wardha scheme to downgrade Muslims, exploit their resources and impose Hindu values, customs, and traditions. The Pirpur Report of 1938, prepared by a committee headed by Raja Muhammad Mehdi, documented alleged discrimination against Muslims, while A.K. Fazlul Huq’s Muslim Suffering Under Congress Rule presented further claims of Muslim grievances. Jinnah turned these grievances into a wider political argument. Addressing the Sindh Provincial Muslim League Conference in Karachi in 1938, he criticised the Congress leadership for its hostile attitude towards the Muslim League. At the League’s Patna session later that year, he argued that Congress rule had further weakened the prospects of a genuine Hindu-Muslim settlement. The resignation of Congress ministries in 1939, following the outbreak of the Second World War, gave Jinnah another opportunity to consolidate Muslim political opinion. He called December 22 the ‘Day of Deliverance’, presenting the end of Congress rule as a moment of political relief for Muslims. Yet the significance of 1937-39 extended beyond immediate grievances. The experience convinced many Muslims that a political system dominated by a permanent majority could threaten their cultural, economic, and political interests. Jinnah responded by reorganising the Muslim League, strengthening its finances and parliamentary machinery, and transforming it from an elite organisation into a mass political movement. The Congress rule thus became an important catalyst in the development of Muslim political consciousness. Under Jinnah’s leadership, the League increasingly transformed Muslim apprehensions into a coherent political demand, ultimately paving the way for the Pakistan Movement. The Lahore Resolution was adopted by the All-India Muslim League at Lahore in its 27th annual session on March 23, 1940. Congress leaders, including Jawaharlal Nehru and Gandhi, opposed the Lahore Resolution, which they termed the “Pakistan Resolution”, arguing that it threatened the idea of a united India. Two years later, in 1942, British minister Sir Stafford Cripps arrived in India to resolve the political deadlock and secure Indian cooperation in the Second World War. His proposals offered India dominion status after the war and the right to frame its own constitution. The Provinces were given the option of not joining the proposed Indian Union, while the princely states were offered participation in the constitutional arrangement. Congress rejected the proposals because it wanted an immediate transfer of power, rather than waiting until after the war. The Muslim League also rejected them, as the scheme did not explicitly recognise its demand for a separate Muslim state. By then, the League was firmly committed to the political direction set by the Lahore Resolution. With the end of WWII in 1945, the British government faced mounting pressure to resolve India’s constitutional crisis. Viceroy Lord Wavell invited the Congress and Muslim League leadership to the Simla Conference, proposing greater transfer of power to Indians while retaining the viceroy as a constitutional head. The conference, however, failed to bridge the differences between Congress and the Muslim League, particularly over Muslim representation. The British subsequently turned to elections to gauge political support. In the 1945-46 elections, the Muslim League achieved a remarkable victory, winning all 30 Muslim-reserved seats in the Central Legislative Assembly and about 95 per cent of the Muslim seats in the provincial legislatures. The results strengthened Jinnah’s claim that the League represented the political aspirations of India’s Muslims and provided a powerful electoral mandate for the demand for a separate homeland. In February 1946, the British government sent the Cabinet Mission, comprising Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander, to negotiate a constitutional settlement. Its plan proposed a relatively weak central government responsible mainly for defence, foreign affairs and communications, while provinces retained substantial autonomy. Although the plan did not fully satisfy the Muslim League’s demand for Pakistan, Jinnah initially saw the reflection of the Two-Nation Theory within its proposed system of provincial groupings. The political crisis deepened when disagreements emerged over the interpretation and implementation of the plan, particularly the grouping of provinces and the formation of an interim government. The Muslim League eventually withdrew its acceptance and called for direct action to press its demand. Jinnah announced Aug 16, 1946 as Direct Action Day. By the end of 1946, the debate over provincial grouping had further sharpened the political divide and Jinnah’s point of view gained immense prominence and increased the momentum for creation of a new country. Since our independence, Pakistan’s record of experimenting with almost every form of government indicates that the successive rulers have failed to understand the Quaid’s vision for statehood. Our history as a nation is replete with political crises that perhaps no other country in the world has experienced because we deviated from Jinnah’s principles, ideals, and vision. Thus, crime and corruption are rapidly becoming a way of life. Aversion to the rule of law, poor governance and economic downfall have become formidable challenges due to inchoate nature of institutions. The political institutions have failed to deliver, and people’s aspirations have not been fulfilled. As a result, people began to shift their loyalties and looked towards alternative religious and ethnic-based platforms which paved the way for undemocratic forces and planted the seeds of extremism, radicalisation, ethnic nationalism, and sectarian violence. These challenges were not properly dealt with by the leadership in the nascent state of Pakistan and thus the feelings of ethnic nationalism permeated both East Pakistan and West Pakistan, which triggered disunity and disintegration. The purpose of the Two-Nation Theory was to create a separate homeland for Muslims. The battle between the Muslim League and Congress was political, not religious. In a 1948 speech the Quaid said: Islam and its idealism have taught democracy, equality, and fair play. After the creation of Pakistan, few world leaders could anticipate that it would be able to survive under the difficult circumstances created by India. On the other hand, it was expected that the Quaid would provide strong leadership, which was badly needed, when he assumed the office of governor-general. He stood like a mighty oak in a storm following independence. His strength was essential for the infant country and no greater fortune could have come to the new country than Jinnah’s acceptance of being its first head of state. Nevertheless, due to the inability of his successors to overcome their disagreements, jealousies, and personal rivalries, it took almost a decade to form the country’s first constitution in 1956, which was abrogated under martial law, imposed in 1958. General Ayub Khan gave a presidential constitution in 1962 and another martial law was imposed in 1969. Later, elections were held in 1970. However, Pakistan faced the tragic separation of East Pakistan. Eventually, after a huge lapse of time, a truly remarkable document — the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan 1973 — was finalised, which has been the basis of Pakistan’s government. The country remained under martial law from 1977 to 1985, with most provisions of the 1973 Constitution held in abeyance. The Ziaul Haq regime (1977-1988) patronised religionisation of politics, created polarisation among various classes in society, encouraged sectarian divide and nurtured extremism. Another authoritarian era — that of Pervez Musharraf (1999-2008) — offered numerous lessons for civilian and military ruling elites. However, the track record of political elites belonging to major political parties in the later decades of democracy indicates that they have not demonstrated a commitment to the rule of law and showed inability to respect the Constitution. Ruling elites remained entrenched in power in violation of the principles and spirit of the Constitution. Thus, the supremacy of the Constitution was compromised. The lack of continuous dialogue among democratic forces to discuss economic and governance issues has caused disillusionment among the masses with the democratic system, which is exposed to vulnerable situation of terrorist insurgencies, socio-economic disparities, and volatile nature of geopolitics under changing dynamics of international politics. These challenges deserve attention of competent, honest, and efficient leadership to deal with the monumental issues confronting Pakistan today, including a fractured political system and economic chaos. Pakistan’s leadership must follow the Quaid’s democratic vision and understand the primacy of Jinnah’s thoughts in tackling constitutional, political, economic and security challenges faced by Pakistan and to come up with a new solution to perennial problems. Our leaders need to promote integration and unity in the country through societal transformation, which requires firm belief in democratic norms and values including liberty, equality, justice, and fair play. There is no reason for anybody to fear democracy, equality of all citizens, inclusivity and cultural diversity. All we need is to be united and make Pakistan a strong nation which should lead the Muslim world towards a peaceful future. The writer is an academic.

According to police in Karachi’s West district, three suspects had been arrested for aerial firing on Independence Day. Incidents of aerial firing are a routine occurrence on occasions such as Independence Day and New Year’s Eve despite bans imposed in the past, often leaving dozens injured . Last year, three people, including a minor girl, were killed and over 100 others wounded in celebratory gunfire across the metropolis at midnight on Independence Day.

Game Review Part 2: Slay the Spire 2 deeply understands what its players want. TL;DR Pros: Closely listens to what fans ask for and provides it Blends creative new features into a tried-and-true formula Alternative Acts make for a less predictable experience Embraces the love for lore with a full expanded universe New allies (and co-op) make the quest less lonely Both new player characters are great, I’ve decided Cons: Still a few stability concerns The Merchant is less talkative now Final score: 6/7 — A game that makes both old and new features pop Reviewed on: PC; available on: Windows, MacOS and Linux (Early Access). Price: $11.99 ( Steam ) This is part 2 of a full review of Slay the Spire 2. You can read Part 1 here . An interesting part of reviewing games is that, no matter how much I enjoy one, it’s difficult to find the energy and motivation to come back to it in my limited free time when I have new ones to try out. I’m happy to report that this is not the case for Slay the Spire 2 , nor even the original Slay the Spire — both are a delightful time-sink and neither has gotten old yet. Having now played more of both games, I have a better appreciation for what StS2 has done with its laurels instead of just sitting on them. In part one of this review, I talked about how the familiar aspects of the first game are elevated in this sequel; this part will focus more on what’s new. I’ve been near-exclusively playing using the two new characters and exploring different playstyles for each. I love the versatility each one has to offer, and the Spire itself contributes something new to the equation with new environments, encounters and even new, powerful Ancients alongside Neow to aid you on your ascent. This is new, too. — GIF via author (A note: Due to personal constraints, I am only reviewing the single player experience of the game. I’m thrilled that co-op questing is now baked into the game, even featuring its own multiplayer-exclusive cards — but it wouldn’t be fair to assess a feature I haven’t yet gotten to try. Those of you readers who have opinions on it, I welcome your thoughts!) Why did it get review bombed? To quickly address a controversy: StS2 has been the victim of more than one review bomb in less than six months, and it’s a shame, because the game is fantastic. From a basic investigation, here’s a summary: the first review bomb related to the removal of some powerful cards for game balancing purposes. The second related to a stir about Anita Sarkeesian — a media critic best known for being a prominent target of the Gamergate harassment campaign — being listed as a consultant in the credits, according to Kotaku . At the risk of sounding dismissive: the cards have since been added back , it’s not 2014 anymore, and I’m a woman who’s a video game critic myself. So I think we can move on and judge the game on its own merits. The Regent: A misleading first impression I’ll admit it: the Regent is finally growing on me. I have a soft spot for characters written to be annoying (sue me), and his mechanics aren’t so bad when you give them a chance. He is pretty obnoxious, though. — screengrab via author Last time, I complained about the use of ‘stars’ to play cards alongside energy. The stars still aren’t my favourite gameplay mechanic, and in my opinion they’re the weakest gimmick of this character. Again, they’re just another type of energy resource, and can actively hinder your run if you don’t have a plan for them. That said, I do appreciate that they function differently from regular energy, not automatically replenishing across turns, so that you’re challenged to strategise a little bit harder and plan ahead of the cards in your hand. Building up energy for later. — GIF via author I can see a world where the stars are only used for a completely separate set of cards, instead of having to work in tandem with energy; or a world where they help provide something different, like a healing mechanic. Either way, this is still a novel mechanic that can be used smartly for some interesting effects. While it takes a bit to get used to, I think the extra strategy and layer of thinking it requires may in fact be what more seasoned players are looking for in the new game, which otherwise may skew a bit easy for a longtime fan. The Regent also comes with some other more fun mechanisms, true to his “outer space ruler” theming to varying degrees. I like his minion attacks for being a very character-specific mechanic — of course this guy would deploy a bunch of servants to die for him — and I especially like his big floating sword that can stack a hefty amount of damage before deploying it all at once for some flashy devastation. Big chop. — GIF via author None of the Regent’s mechanics are subtle or sneaky; they’re an in-your-face show of might, which I think suits his character perfectly. I do wish that, true to his kingliness, he’d start his ascents with a little more money than other characters for the sake of flavour — they can be balanced out in other ways to keep things fair. The Necrobinder: My new best friend The Necrobinder remains a fantastic new addition to the Spire’s cast, as does her familiar Osty. Everything from her design to her personality and lore is instantly compelling — you simply cannot go wrong with “vengeful flaming skeleton sorcerer”, and she’s a girlboss to boot! A+, Anita. Who doesn’t love a revenge quest? — screengrab via author Mechanically, I love how her battle style embraces her Grim Reaper vibe with effects like ‘doom’ —enhanced by pleasant visuals of enemies being dragged back into the ground from whence they came — while simultaneously keeping it light with a big, loyal, Addams Family -esque pet hand that would (and will constantly) die for you. Your time has come… — GIF via author Like the Regent, the Necrobinder has a versatile skillset, which allows for a lot of variation in builds. I’m always a big fan of stacking status effects — with the Silent, for example, it’s poison, and here it’s piling on huge amounts of doom to literally send enemies to an early grave. I also really, really enjoy any run where I can find an interesting use for Osty, who can potentially be a glass cannon with an attack build, buff your other cards by constantly dying, or stack a respectable amount of health and become a formidable shield if you play your cards right. He protecc. — GIF via author He attacc. — GIF via author But most importantly, he bounces right bacc. — GIF via author Fun fights, alternate acts and fresh faces I’ve been really enjoying what the new bosses have to offer. In some cases, they take clear inspiration from clever, successful ideas in the first game (looking at you, Kaiser Crab), while in others they throw in new powers and gimmicks that are both fresh and really fun. This feels familiar… — GIF via author Still a really fun fight. — GIF via author Also, maybe the best decision the new game makes is the addition of new regions that can start being unlocked not long into the game, which serve as alternative versions of each Act. I love this choice. Not only does it provide some extra randomness to each run once you’re ready, but it keeps each ascent from being too predictable with the kinds of monsters it’s going to throw at you. In particular, I’m a huge fan of the Underdocks, the alternative version of Act 1, which leans hard into its nautical theming with enemies that are seaweedy, seafoody or just plain wet — enhanced by some great animations and vibrant use of colour. Seaweed. — GIF via author Seafood. — GIF via author Wet. — GIF via author Additionally, Neow isn’t the only age-old deity swimming around in the Spire anymore: new Ancients are unlocked as you progress, joining other NPCs that greet you between Acts with specialised powerups to boost you along. Unlike the big ol’ chest of relics you used to see after a boss fight, these guys actually talk to you, and they have a lot of personality. A powerful ally. — screengrab via author An unlockable deity. — screengrab via author I think what I like the most about all these characters is that, unlike the first game, your ascents don’t feel so lonely anymore. There’s always a guarantee of meeting interesting and powerful allies as you go— even though the Merchant regrettably doesn’t talk much now, which makes me sad. I miss our conversations, but at least he’s there. Guess he doesn’t like my haircut anymore… — GIF via author Lore for days The timeline is a great way for the Spire duology to embrace enthusiasm for the lore behind the universe by fleshing it out further. Alongside the existence of the official multiplayer mode, I think this stands as a perfect example of the creators showing that they paid attention to the reception of StS1 and what people enjoyed, without coming off as an obvious or desperate move to bait fans. They know what the people want, and it’s storytelling. Lore! — GIF via author The timeline has two additional strengths. Firstly, it unlocks new epochs (entries) based on not only progress but on players’ initiative: seeking out Elites (minibosses) to fight or using certain characters, for example, becomes easier when you’re motivated by the reward of unlocking lore you otherwise wouldn’t. Fine, I’ll stop being a coward. — screengrab via author Secondly, it adds a new dimension of colour to the usual unlocking of new cards, relics and characters. Not only can I always see how much more there still is to discover about the world, but it’s visually and narratively much more striking than it used to be to discover it. When you put it so enticingly… — GIF via author I should note here that many epochs still contain placeholder thumbnails for their artwork, which is just one of those Early Access things to accept about an otherwise super-polished game. That said, I don’t mind at all, because they’re endearing and make me laugh. It’s alright, I see the vision. — screengrab via author Overall, I like the new direction the creators have taken by building on the narrative aspect of the game. I don’t even mind the overly wordy text boxes anymore — although they were jarring at first, I think they actually suit the new storytelling-heavy vibes really well. Cheese. — screengrab via author Verdict: Honours the old and nails the new What still needs fixing? Not very much, I’m amazed to say. I’m super impressed by how well put together this game is for Early Access, at least in single player mode — though I did experience my only crash while trying to simply look at multiplayer-specific cards in the Compendium. For a solo player, I can say with confidence that it already provides a smooth and fun gameplay experience. I could still get behind the reworking of some cards and mechanics, particularly those of the Regent, but I’m glad I gave him a chance to prove his worth as a player character. While I miss the Merchant’s chronic yapping, I’m still happy to see him. And so far, just about every major change StS2 has made to the original game has been a good one, adding new elements to a tried-and-true formula and listening closely to player feedback. As I mentioned in the previous part of this review, I was completely new to deckbuilders before the Spire duology. I can now confidently recommend either of these games as a first deckbuilder for anyone who wants to give them a try. And if you already like them? I promise you’re in for a treat. A rest at the docks. — GIF via author .single.story { background-image: url('https://i.dawn.com/primary/2026/08/13205950a22d551.webp'); background-repeat: repeat-y; background-attachment: fixed; background-size: 100vw 100vh; } body:not(.newskit) .story { color: #ffffff; } .story a { color: #ff9d1f !important; } article.box, .story .template__main { background: #000000; opacity: 0.97; } article.box { padding: 5px; border: 0; } .story__time { color: #aaa; } .story__title, .comments { background: #000000; padding: 10px; }

President Zardari approves summoning of NA, Senate sessions on August 17. In a post on the social media platform X, the President’s Secretariat said, “The president has approved the awarding of military honours to 1,172 personnel from the armed forces and civil armed forces.” “The president has approved summoning the National Assembly session on August 17 at 5pm and the Senate session at 4pm,” it added. Pakistan's leadership stresses need for unity, reforms as nation celebrates Independence Day. Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership has stressed the need for unity and reforms as the nation celebrates 79 years of independence today. According to state-run Radio Pakistan , the day dawned with a 31-gun salute in Islamabad and a 21-gun salute at the provincial headquarters. A change of guards ceremony was also held at the mausoleum of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah in Karachi. ‘Pakistan’s security linked to peace in our neighbourhood’ In his message, President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to Quaid-i-Azam, those behind the Pakistan Movement and those who sacrificed their homes, security and livelihoods in the struggle for a homeland. “But independence is not only a historic achievement. It is also a responsibility that each generation must carry forward. The Pakistan that was created through the democratic will of its people must continue to grow stronger, more secure and more prosperous. Our task is not only to remember what earlier generations achieved, but to add to it through our own work,” he said. The president said that the past year had reminded citizens of the strength of the Pakistani nation. Recalling last year’s brief military conflict with India, he said, “The events surrounding Marka-i-Haq demonstrated that Pakistan seeks peace, but also possesses the resolve and capacity to defend its sovereignty and national interests. The lesson of strength is ultimately a lesson of responsibility. A country that can defend itself must also use its strength to prevent conflict, protect peace and serve the interests of its people.” He said that the security and stability enjoyed today had come at a great cost, paying tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces, law enforcement agencies and police. “Their courage and commitment have helped safeguard our nation against external aggression and the threat of terrorism. The people of Pakistan remain deeply grateful for their service,” he said. He also highlighted Pakistan’s efforts to facilitate dialogue in the region. “Pakistan has effectively used its channels of communication, its geographical location and diplomatic capital to encourage dialogue and de-escalation at a time when wider conflict could have serious consequences for the region and the world,” he said. He reiterated that all disputes must be ultimately addressed through dialogue and diplomacy. “Our security is linked to the peace and stability of our neighbourhood and the world at large. Pakistan will continue to support efforts that reduce tensions, protect regional stability and create conditions for cooperation,” he said. The president also went on to say that the country must focus on the work that will determine Pakistan’s future. “We must strengthen our economy, create greater opportunities for our young people, improve education and skills, strengthen institutions through a series of governance, economic and social reforms to ensure that the benefits of development and democracy reach every part and community of the country,” he said. “Pakistan’s greatest strength is its young people. Across the country and around the world, they are demonstrating their talent in science, technology, business, education and the creative industries. Our responsibility is to give them the education, skills and opportunities they need to realise their potential. By investing in our youth today, we are investing in Pakistan’s future,” he added. “For ordinary Pakistanis, national progress is measured in practical terms. It means a young person finding the skills and opportunity to build a career. It means a family being able to access quality education and healthcare. It means farmers, workers, traders and businesses being able to plan for the future with greater confidence. The strength of Pakistan will ultimately be judged by whether our national progress improves the lives of its people,” President Zardari said. He also voiced Pakistan’s support for the people of occupied Kashmir, saying Pakistan will continue to support a peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with the aspirations of its people and the relevant United Nations resolutions. On Afghanistan, the president said that Pakistan had always respected and supported the national sovereignty of our neighbour Afghanistan and expected the same reciprocity. “It is sad that the current interim regime of Afghanistan is allowing and supporting a cocktail of terror groups to use their soil for launching attacks against neighbouring countries including Pakistan. It is sad the Taliban regime of Afghanistan is collaborating with India in launching terror attacks against Pakistani civilians and security personnel. They are doing this to distract us from the peace building efforts of Pakistan, recognised by the entire world,” he said. “I warn them to stop these evil actions against the people of Pakistan and assure all and sundry that the armed forces of Pakistan are capable of defeating these evil designs,” he said. He ended his message by calling on the nation to contribute to the country’s progress in whatever field they serve. ‘Pakistan committed to defending its national interests’ Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also began his message by paying tribute to the founding leaders of Pakistan, saying the nation owed the fulfilment of its dream of an independent homeland to their vision, statesmanship and sacrifices. Highlighting the government’s economic achievements over the past two-and-a-half years, PM Shehbaz said the country had successfully navigated challenging circumstances to achieve economic stability and was now moving towards becoming a developed economy. He noted that remittances from overseas Pakistanis had increased by $11.3 billion over the past two years, which he termed a reflection of their confidence in government policies. The prime minister said harnessing modern information technology, promoting innovation-driven industrial and agricultural development, creating employment opportunities and establishing a world-class education and skills system remained among the government’s top priorities. Paying tribute to the armed forces, the prime minister said the military, under the leadership of Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, had demonstrated exemplary unity and courage during Marka-i-Haq, adding another chapter to the country’s history of defence. He said Pakistan remained committed to defending its national interests, including its right to water resources, and reiterated that the country would continue to play its role as a responsible nation and a stabilising force for regional and global peace. He cited the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as testimony to the country’s growing strategic role in the region. The prime minister also expressed solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir and the Palestinian people. He said lasting peace in South Asia was contingent upon a diplomatic resolution of the Kashmir dispute in line with United Nations resolutions, international law and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people. The prime minister also paid tribute to the martyrs of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies who sacrificed their lives for the country, and called upon all segments of society, particularly political parties, to work together for national unity, integrity and the advancement of national interests. He concluded his message by praying for Pakistan’s continued progress and dignity in the comity of nations. ‘Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity of its people’ CDF Munir, Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf and Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu also issued a message to mark Independence Day. According to Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the armed forces paid tribute to the Quaid and those whose sacrifices resulted in a sovereign Pakistan. “Their vision, courage and resolve remain a guiding force for the nation and continue to inspire us to uphold the principles and ideals of Pakistan,” the statement said. “The armed forces of Pakistan respectfully acknowledge the supreme sacrifices of our martyrs, the services of our veterans, the dedication of law enforcement personnel and the contributions of every Pakistani who has served the nation. Their courage and selfless service have bolstered Pakistan’s resilience and safeguarded its independence, security and national interests,” it added. “As guardians of Pakistan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, the armed forces reaffirm their unwavering resolve to defend the motherland against all threats, uphold the Constitution and discharge the sacred trust reposed in them by the people of Pakistan. United with the nation, the armed forces will remain steadfast in preserving peace and stability while creating an environment conducive to national progress and prosperity,” the statement said. “Pakistan’s strength lies in the unity and collective resolve of its people. On this Independence Day, let us renew our commitment to the enduring principles of faith, unity and discipline, strengthen national cohesion, promote tolerance and work together towards a secure, stable and prosperous Pakistan,” it concluded. Dar reaffirms determination to safeguard country’s sovereignty In his message on the occasion, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar recalled Marka-i-Haq and reaffirmed Pakistan’s determination to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. “We commemorated the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, recalling Pakistan’s resolute and successful response to Indian aggression in 2025,” he said in a televised address to the nation. “The occasion reaffirmed our determination to safeguard Pakistan’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity while remaining firmly committed to international law, responsible state craft and the pursuit of regional peace.” At the outset of his address, the deputy PM extended greetings to Pakistanis and expatriates on the Independence Day, saying we commemorate the day “to pay tribute to Quaid-i-Azam whose visionary leadership, unwavering resolve and steadfast commitment transformed the aspirations for a separate homeland into reality”. He also paid honour to the leaders and workers of the Pakistan movement whose “courage, dedication and countless sacrifices laid the foundations of our independent state”. Dar said that since independence, the country had made “remarkable strides across diverse fields guided by the enduring principles of unity, faith and discipline”. “Today we are a resilient nation of more than 250 million people bound together by our shared history, collective heritage and common aspirations,” he added. He also noted that the country’s achievements in education, science and technology, economic development, sports, culture and other fields “reflect the talent, determination and immense potential of our people”. The deputy PM also mentioned Pakistan’s “strengthened” position on the international stage over the past eight decades. “Our expanding diplomatic engagement, growing economic connectivity and partnerships, and deepening defence and security cooperation reflect Pakistan’s confidence and its commitment to contributing to a peaceful stable and prosperous region and world.” He also mentioned the defence accord signed by Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia last week, saying the “historic agreement reflects our shared resolve to deepen strategic cooperation, strengthen collective security and addresses evolving regional and international peace and security challenges”. He also paid special tribute to armed forces, police and paramilitary forces of the country, saying their “courage, professionalism and unwavering commitment remain a bulwark of our national security”. Dar noted the country always “stood for peace, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect among nations”. He referred to last year’s conflict with India and said the events “underscored the urgent need of peaceful resolution of longstanding disputes, particularly the Jammu and Kashmir dispute which remains a source of instability in our region”. “Pakistan will continue to extend its principles, moral, political and diplomatic support to the Kashmiri people in their just struggle for the realisation of their right to self-determination in accordance with the relevant UNSC resolutions,” he added. On the occasion, he urged people to “draw renewed inspirations from the ideals and vision that led to the creation of Pakistan”. “Let us reaffirm our collective resolve to strengthen our institutions, uphold our national unity, harness the potential of our people and build a stronger more prosperous and peaceful Pakistan for generations to come,” he concluded.

Nigel Farage regains UK parliamentary seat, fights off Count Binface challenge. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage regained his parliamentary seat on Friday in an election he triggered to bolster his position against allegations of financial impropriety, a strategy that was undermined when his main challenger, a comedian dressed as a trash can, won more than a quarter of the vote. Farage, one of Britain’s leading Brexit campaigners, in a highly unusual move did not turn up at the count in the southern English seaside resort of Clacton because he said the police had advised him that there was a campaign to disrupt the result. “I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory … and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies,” Farage told supporters at a party before the result was announced. The election was triggered after Farage resigned from parliament last month to seek a fresh mandate from voters in what he described as a war against an establishment bent on discrediting him over taking undeclared gifts from donors. After Britain’s main parties pulled out of the race, calling it a self-serving stunt, Farage’s main challenger ended up being Count Binface, a figure created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has become a fixture of fun at British elections. While Farage took 62.8 per cent of the vote, Count Binface, whose policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using a speakerphone on public transport, secured 26.7pc. Reform’s momentum shows signs of slowing After enjoying a lengthy lead in the opinion polls, Reform has seen its popularity wane, driven partly by the funding accusations made against Farage, who is under investigation in parliament over whether he should have declared a 5 million ($6.75m) gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire investor. After declaring his decision to trigger the election in Clacton little more than a ploy to distract from those allegations, other British parties pulled out of the race, leaving even some of Farage’s strongest supporters questioning whether the veteran politician had been wrong-footed. Laura Richards-Gray, a politics lecturer at Birkbeck University in London, said the absence of major-party opponents undermined his attempt to turn it into what he called a “people versus the establishment” contest. “This has backfired, particularly nationally, as Farage lost control of the narrative,” she said, adding some voters saw the election as “a waste of time and money”. Farage’s position has not been helped by a rise in support for the governing Labour Party. Since Andy Burnham became prime minister last month, Labour has been enjoying a bounce in ratings, with the party leading Reform 28pc to 25pc. Burnham has dominated the airwaves and social media in his first few weeks in office, and while the next national election is expected in three years’ time, he appears to be consolidating a left-leaning bloc around Labour. Reform, on the other hand, is competing for a divided right-wing vote with the Conservative Party and the anti-immigration party Restore Britain gaining in support. Gift from billionaire crypto investor Despite winning this vote, the parliamentary watchdog is expected to continue its investigation into his financial declarations once he returns to parliament. At the heart of the investigation is whether he should have declared the gift from a Thailand-based billionaire before the 2024 national election. Under parliamentary rules, members of parliament must declare any donations received in the year preceding an election within one month of taking office. Farage has admitted receiving the money, but not declaring it, saying he has done nothing wrong because it was a personal gift. If the parliamentary authorities, who are investigating, conclude that Farage breached declaration rules, he could face a suspension from parliament, and another vote to retain his seat, where the main parties would probably field candidates.

The future of fitness tracking is going analog—sort of. These days, pursuing health and fitness goals doesn’t just require personalized physical training and a well-planned diet. For many, it also involves smart technology as a dependable companion. We have seen it in the form of innovative gym equipment and other wearables, such as rings and smartwatches, designed to monitor health and wellness metrics. Smartwatches remain the most common, offering users a convenient way to track everything from heart rate and daily activity to sleep and exercise. But as consumers become more conscious of their relationship with technology, a new generation of wearables is taking a quieter approach—one that prioritizes health tracking without placing another screen on the wrist. This is where Garmin’s newest offering steps in. Dubbed the Cirqa Smart Band, this latest health and fitness tracker is designed to collect data throughout the day and let you review everything later. The catch is that it doesn’t have a screen. With no notifications, it quietly records your data, which you can access via the Garmin Connect app with no subscription required. “With its discreet design and trusted health and fitness tracking tools Garmin is known for, this smart band complements our lineup of popular smartwatches and wellness monitors, allowing users to transition smoothly between their Garmin devices throughout the day,” says Susan Lyman, Garmin vice president of Consumer Sales and Marketing. “Plus, with no subscription required, Cirqa Smart Band helps you stay on top of your health and fitness goals—and makes a thoughtful gift for others who want to do the same.” Think of it as an analog approach, sort of, to a modern health and fitness tracker. It is a fabric band one can wear on the wrist or arm and monitors heart rate, stress, sleep stages, workouts and activity, and recovery time, among others. The Cirqa Smart Band is one of the things Garmin highlighted when it unveiled its flagship store in the Philippines last July 30 at SM Megamall in Mandaluyong City. To note, the store isn’t just the biggest one in the country but also the largest flagship store in Southeast Asia. Much like the Cirqa Smart Band, the store features a lot of new experiences for fans of the brand to try. Among its highlights is the Garmin Golf Lab, a dedicated space equipped with golf simulators that allows golfers to experience performance insights through real-time data. Cycling enthusiasts can also explore Garmin's Cycling Ecosystem, featuring an integrated setup of cycling computers and wearables that demonstrates how Garmin technologies work together to support every ride. “People will have a good experience in trying all the products here,” Sky Chen, Garmin Southeast Asia regional director, tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle. “We can bring all the products we have here, from the simulated golf experience to the smallest smartwatch in the world (Garmin Lily 2) and the ultrathin GPS fitness smartwatch (Venu X1).” Visitors can also explore Garmin's latest innovations, including the recently launched Forerunner 170 and Forerunner 70, alongside Garmin's broader portfolio of fitness, wellness, outdoor, and lifestyle products. “This flagship store is more than a place to shop. It's a space where people can experience Garmin products firsthand, connect with the community, and find inspiration to pursue their goals,” Sky says. “Whether you're training for your next race, improving your golf game, exploring the outdoors, or simply looking to live a healthier lifestyle, we want this store to be a destination for the growing Garmin community in the Philippines.” The Cirqa Smart Band will be available beginning Aug. 14 at Garmin Brand Stores, Garmin Specialty Stores, The Loop, and Garmin's official e-commerce platforms.

The suspensions covered various grade levels in public and private schools, with some local governments shifting to Alternative Delivery Mode (ADM) while others called off only afternoon face-to-face classes. In Manila, classes from kindergarten to senior high school in public and private schools were suspended, with learning activities shifted to ADM. Valenzuela City and Malabon City suspended classes at all levels in public and private schools and shifted learning activities to ADM. Mandaluyong City suspended classes from preschool to Grade 12, including those under the Alternative Learning System (ALS). In Pasig City, classes from kindergarten to senior high school, as well as those in Day Care/Early Childhood Development Centers and ALS, were suspended, with learning activities shifted to ADM. Marikina City and San Juan City suspended classes at all levels in public and private schools, while Pateros called off classes from preschool to senior high school in both public and private schools. In Makati City, face-to-face classes at all levels in both public and private schools were suspended. Quezon City suspended afternoon face-to-face classes in public schools covering learners in Child Development Centers, kindergarten, Grades 1 to 12, and ALS. In Caloocan City, afternoon classes at all levels in public and private schools were suspended due to continuous rains brought by the habagat, with classes shifted to ADM. Las Piñas City also suspended classes at all levels in public and private schools. Navotas City suspended all f ace-to-face classes at all levels in public and private schools beginning 12 noon on Friday, with schools shifting to alternative delivery modes, including online, asynchronous, or modular learning. Meanwhile, in nearby Rizal province, Taytay suspended all afternoon face-to-face classes at all levels in public and private schools due to the expected continued rainfall and a Yellow Heavy Rainfall Advisory in the province. Classes in Taytay shifted to Alternative Modes of Delivery of Learning (AMDL), based on the learning arrangements of individual schools. In Bulacan, 24 local government units also suspended face-to-face classes at all levels in public and private schools amid the prevailing weather conditions. The affected areas were Angat, Balagtas, Baliwag, Bocaue, Bulakan, Bustos, Calumpit, Doña Remedios Trinidad, Guiguinto, Hagonoy, Malolos, Marilao, Meycauayan, Norzagaray, Obando, Pandi, Paombong, Plaridel, Pulilan, San Ildefonso, San Jose del Monte, San Miguel, San Rafael, and Santa Maria. Local governments continued to monitor flood-prone communities, waterways, and other areas vulnerable to prolonged rainfall as the habagat persisted over Metro Manila and nearby provinces. (With reports from Manila Bulletin Metro Team)

Aussie teams, La Salle, AdU, Perpetual in Roxas City Invt’l. Two visiting teams from Australia and three collegiate squads from the UAAP and NCAA clash from Aug. 21 to 26 when the first ever Roxas City Invitational Tournament 2026 kicks off at the Dinggoy Roxas Civic Center in Capiz. Bannering the Land Down Under are sports and education institutions Brian Kerle Academy from Brisbane and the Universal Athlete Centre from Keysborough in Melbourne. Several mainstays from Australia’s NBL1 are expected in the rosters of both teams. Representing UAAP are the De La Salle Green Archers and the Adamson Soaring Falcons, while waving the NCAA flag are the Perpetual Altas. Roxas City Mayor Ronnie T. Dadivas heads the organizing committee of this historic event, along with executive director Miggy Dadivas and veteran tournament organizer Van Halen Parmis. Mike Reyes is the tournament commissioner with former PBA chairman Buddy Encarnado serving as league consultant. “In line with its goal of growing the sport at the grassroots level, the tournament, organized in Roxas City for the first time, will run community outreach programs alongside the main competition, including basketball clinics for local youth led by the visiting and participating teams,” said Mayor Dadivas. “The tournament will also conduct refresher courses for local referees, led by the technical head in coordination with the referee coordinator from Australia.” Former PBA players, notably Jireh Ibanes, Ogie Menor and Glenn Peter Yap, trace their roots to Roxas City, also considered the Seafood Capital of the Philippines. All games will be streamed live via Facebook and YouTube. Roxas City is the capital of Capiz, a province located on the northeast part of Panay Island in the Western Visayas region.

Duterte camp seeks oral arguments on motion to quash grave threats cases. The legal team of Vice President Sara Duterte is seeking oral arguments on her motion to quash the grave threats cases filed against her before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court. In a press statement on Friday, August 14, Duterte’s counsel, Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim, said the defense is filing a manifestation emphasizing the need for oral arguments because of what it described as the “far-reaching consequences” of the cases. “The defense is now filing a manifestation emphasizing the need for oral arguments on the Vice President’s motion to quash, considering the far-reaching consequences of the Grave Threats cases,” Lim said. Lim argued that allowing the criminal prosecution of a sitting Vice President could have broader implications for other impeachable officials. “If a sitting Vice President may be indicted and prosecuted, then other incumbent impeachable officers such as the Ombudsman, members of the Constitutional Commissions, Supreme Court Justices, and even the President, may also be indicted and prosecuted,” he said. Lim is counsel for Duterte in the grave threats cases being handled by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI). Dismissal of grave threats cases sought Duterte’s lawyers earlier filed a motion to quash the information against the Vice President, citing lack of jurisdiction. The Department of Justice (DOJ) filed three counts of grave threats against Duterte before the Quezon City RTC on August 11 over statements she made in November 2024 involving President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and then-House Speaker Martin Romualdez. The cases stem from Duterte’s remarks during an online press conference in which she said she had arranged for someone to kill Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez if she herself were killed. The NBI investigated the matter and recommended criminal charges. Prosecutors later found probable cause to pursue the grave threats cases. No reported arrest warrant against Duterte Amid rumors circulating online that Duterte may be arrested, there is no publicly reported warrant of arrest against the Vice President in connection with the grave threats cases as of August 14. The current proceedings remain focused on Duterte’s motion to quash, which the Quezon City court will have to resolve as the case moves forward. The filing of the cases does not automatically mean that an arrest warrant has been issued. Lim’s latest statement likewise does not say that a warrant has been issued or that an arrest is imminent. Instead, the defense is asking the court to hear oral arguments on the jurisdictional issue and the broader constitutional implications it sees in prosecuting an incumbent impeachable officer. Issue involving other impeachable officials raised Lim’s argument centers on whether an incumbent impeachable officer can be subjected to criminal prosecution while still holding office. The defense said the issue could affect not only Duterte but also other officials who are constitutionally subject to impeachment, including the President, the Ombudsman, members of the Constitutional Commissions, and Supreme Court justices. The Quezon City RTC will ultimately determine whether the criminal cases may proceed and how it will resolve Duterte’s motion to quash. Jojie Lloren’s new venture features pieces to wear, keep, and pass on. Jojie Lloren has his way of making women feel elegant and confident through the way he designs his pieces. His collections are always poetic, merging narratives with precise techniques, resulting in pieces that feel both deeply personal and timeless. That’s Jojie as a designer: he is always a giver. He gives pieces of himself through every collection, sharing his stories, his craftsmanship, and his deep appreciation for the women who wear his clothes. His generosity also extends to his role as a mentor, honing the skills of young designers and sharing the knowledge and experience he has gained throughout his career. This time, he is combining his mission of creating purposeful garments and supporting emerging creatives as he unveils his newest project: J. Lloren Editions. Its goal is to create collectible luxury garments that embody artistic excellence, cultural significance, and enduring craftsmanship. “I've spent most of my career making couture, creating one garment at a time for one person at a time. Every piece was made with care because I knew exactly who it was for. Over the years, I started asking myself if there was a way to bring that same level of craftsmanship to more people without losing what made it special,” Jojie says. “At the same time, I kept meeting incredibly talented Filipino artists who deserved more opportunities than they were getting,” the designer adds. “That made me wonder: What if a garment could be more than something you wear? What if it could also become a way for an artist's work to reach people in a different way?” This is where J. Lloren Editions steps in. The series features limited-edition ready-to-wear pieces made in collaboration with some of the Philippines’ emerging creatives. For its inaugural collection, Jojie taps visual artist and printmaker Joey Cobcobo, photographer and visual artist Kim Montes, and Vicky Vizcarra Amalingan, Rita Nazareno, and Reese Rivilla of SC Vizcarra, mounting lines that feature collectible works, honor collaboration, and preserve cultural heritage. J. Lloren Editions is the veteran designer’s way of redefining luxury. The Canvas Series honors the work of Joey, where art, fashion, and craftsmanship come together. Kim brings her distinctive eye to the first edition of the Lens Series, where photography becomes more than documentation. Lastly, the women of SC Vizcarra explore how weaving, fashion, and design can converge into collectible pieces that honor heritage while embracing modern luxury. “Every J. Lloren Editions piece has a story behind it. It's made in very limited numbers and carries a piece of Filipino creativity,” Jojie muses. “Every design is strictly limited to just 12 pieces. To support exhibitions and special presentations, only an initial three to six pieces are produced. The remaining pieces are created on a made-to-order basis, ensuring that every garment is crafted only when there is a collector waiting to own it.” Apart from collaborating with creatives and mindful manufacturing, J. Lloren Editions also spotlights the Artist Fund, Jojie’s long-term commitment to supporting Filipino creatives. The fund ensures that every purchase contributes directly to sustaining the Philippine creative community. A portion of proceeds from every edition contributes to initiatives that may include artist royalties, creative grants, residency opportunities, and mentorship programs, among others. “What I hope is that, years from now, these pieces will still mean something to the people who own them,” the designer says. “Not just as clothes from a particular collection, but as a reminder of the artists and makers who came together to create them.”

Affordable HMO now accessible to millions of Filipinos via GCash and KwikCare. To help Filipinos stay protected from unforeseen medical costs and access affordable, quality healthcare, GCash and KwikCare are partnering to offer the first health maintenance organization (HMO) coverage directly available from the GCash app. For millions of Filipinos, quality healthcare remains a luxury out of reach, leaving families highly vulnerable to unexpected medical crises. Recent data highlights a stark reality: 64% of Filipino families cannot afford a ₱10,000 hospital bill without falling into debt¹, while 30% of households live on the brink of financial distress with sudden health shocks acting as a major driver of this vulnerability². This challenge is most especially felt among MSME workers, gig economy freelancers, and part-time earners who lack traditional corporate HMO benefits, leaving them just “one sickness away from poverty.” To break this cycle, democratizing healthcare is critical. By making health coverage proactive, affordable, and accessible at the grassroots level, Filipino breadwinners can protect both their health and their hard-earned financial stability. GCash, through its in-app insurance platform GInsure, has partnered with KwikCare to offer digital-first HMO coverage through a flexible monthly subscription. The offering does not require large upfront costs, long-term commitments, or complicated paperwork. Users can sign up in minutes, making healthcare coverage easily accessible. Through GInsure, KwikCare offers monthly HMO plans designed to make healthcare coverage more adaptable to different needs and circumstances. Starting at ₱995 per month, the service provides access to inpatient, outpatient, emergency, and laboratory services, along with cashless access to more than 2,000 accredited healthcare providers nationwide, and benefits of up to ₱350,000, with additional personal accident coverage of up to ₱1 million. Moreover, the offering also allows users to add their family members. “Filipinos deserve the peace of mind that comes with reliable health coverage. When breadwinners and their families can better access essential health services as well as manage unexpected medical emergencies without worrying about the costs, we're protecting not just their health, but their financial future,” shared Winsley Bangit, Group Head of New Business at Mynt, the parent company of GCash. “Our mission has always been to make quality healthcare more accessible to every Filipino. Through our partnership with GCash, we're bringing reliable HMO coverage closer to millions by making it available through a platform they already use every day,” emphasized Hamilton Angluben, Chief Executive Officer of KwikCare. “We believe digital distribution is one of the most powerful ways to expand healthcare access and help more families protect both their health and their financial future.” To sign up for a KwikCare HMO plan, GCash users can open the GCash app, navigate to “Explore the App”, select “GInsure”, and tap the “HMO” icon. After completing their enrollment, their login credentials will be sent to their registered email address and mobile number within 15 days. Once their KwikCare plan is active, users need to download the Amaphil app on Google Play Store and Apple App Store to access their healthcare benefits, such as booking consultations, requesting letters of authorization, and viewing partner hospitals. Meanwhile, they can continue to manage their HMO subscription through the GCash app, including paying their monthly premiums and accessing other account management features via the My GInsure tab. As more Filipinos turn to digital platforms to manage their everyday finances, GCash and KwikCare are making health protection just as accessible. Through GInsure, the partnership empowers Filipinos to conveniently manage their health coverage, protect their savings from unforeseen medical costs, and navigate their healthcare needs with greater confidence. For more information, visit https://www.gcash.com.

DPWH reports P1.4 billion initial damage to roads in Cordillera. BAGUIO CITY – The Department of Public Works and Highways-Cordillera reported an initial P1,454,897,648 damage to roads wrought by typhoons Luis, Maymay, and the habagat. According to Engr. Patrick Cerilo, of DPWH-CAR, a total of 186 road sections were affected in the entire region, with 179 landslides recorded since the beginning of August. These sections were affected by landslides or road cuts, road slips, fallen trees, and aggravated road slips. Cerilo shared that the number of road landslides recorded this August has exceeded the historical average of about 160 landslides recorded from 2015 to 2021. Most of the landslides were recorded in Benguet. A total of 13 road sections are still closed, including eight national roads, such as the entire stretch of Kennon Road which is open for residents only for now; Baguio-Itogon Road at Poblacion, Itogon; Benguet-Nueva Vizcaya Road in Bekel, La Trinidad; Tawang-Ambiong Road at Ambiong, La Trinidad; Abatan-Mankayan-Cervantes Road at Tabio, Mankayan; Banaue Hungduan-Benguet Boundary Road at Hapao, Hungduan; Banaue via Tanudan-Barlig Road at Dupligan, Tanudan; and Mt. Province-Ilocos Sur Road via Tue Road in Balaoa, Tadian. The Gov. Bado Dangwa National Road in Ampusongan, Bakun, is open for light vehicles only. He said the DPWH is currently installing safety devices and conducting clearing operations. They are also assessing the damages and preparing documents for their repair and funding. "Let's be careful. If our trip is not important, let's not travel. Even though the effect of the southwest monsoon is subsiding, there are, and there will be landslides," Cerilo appealed.

Biggest and most immersive MaArte Fair at the Pen yet, 'Karnabal,' happening in August. One of the country’s biggest gatherings of Filipino artisan-entrepreneurs is back at The Peninsula Manila from August 13-16. Now on its 17th staging, the MaArte Fair at the Pen has become an annual must-go-to event for discerning Filipino shoppers who are passionate about uniquely Filipino creativity, the evolution of traditional Filipino artisanship, and both preserving our cultural heritage as well as making it relevant in the 21st century. This year features the biggest gathering yet of some of most recognized names in bespoke Filipino design and craftsmanship, many of whom have grown with the MaArte Fair since 2009. It will also be welcoming a bumper crop of up-and-coming entrepreneurs, making for a mix of oNerings that have made it a consistent favorite, among Metro Manila’s who’s who. This year’s theme Karnabal will be a whimsical, nostalgic, yet a contemporary reimaging of the iconic Manila Carnival—an annual event that was held from 1908 to 1939. It has since been inextricably woven into Philippine culture and lives on today as the ubiquitous Perya. MaArte Fair’s Karnabal vibrantly brings together culture, community, and creativity in service of a greater cause. The MaArte Fair is the flagship fundraising event of the Museum Foundation of the Philippines (MFPI), a private non-profit organization committed to the preservation of Philippine cultural heritage. A portion of the fair’s proceeds are issued as grants to deserving organizations or individuals engaged in cultural preservation projects. “Karnabal is our way of turning the fairgrounds into a living tribute to a piece of Filipino history that many younger genearions have only heard about in passing,” said Danny C. Jacinto, President of the Museum Foundation of the Philippines (MFPI). “Every exhbitor here is helping us keep that story – and the artisians who carry it forward – alive for the next generation.” For MaArte Fair 2026, returning MaArte mainstays such as Happy Andrada, PamPinay, A.Mara, and OneWeave will provide the event's remarkable staying power, while an influx of pioneering new exhibitors— namely Genes & Hails, Locallaé, Lookal by Alixia Marie, Ligaw Travel Accessories, Dermtropics, Mele + Marie, and Fam PH—inject a fresh sense of excitement, novelty, and even mystery. This year's event is co-sponsored by the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) and GCash for Business, reflecting their shared commitment to preserving the Philippines' cultural heritage. As part of its sponsorship, BPI also oNers exclusive privileges for its clients, making the experience even more rewarding while celebrating the country's rich history and culture. The fair’s celebratory atmosphere is also in line with the 50th Anniversary of The Peninsula Manila, which will be the home of the MaArte Fair for the 8th time. For more information, go to: https://museumfoundationph.org/maarte-fair

80 houses destroyed in Zamboanga fire. ZAMBOANGA CITY- Some 80 houses were destroyed here when a fire swept through Cambodia Purok 1, Sangali at dawn on Friday, August 14. The fire started at 1:21am and swept through the densely-packed neighborhood where houses are made of light materials. The fire reached the third alarm and was placed under control at 2:44am. It was extinguished an hour later. The Bureau of Fire Protection initially assessed the damage at P1.44-million. The City Social Welfare and Development office is conducting its assessment of the situation. Initial data showed that around 100 families were affected by the fire.

2 nabbed in Pasay computer shop drug bust; P1.02-M shabu seized. A drug deal inside a computer shop in Pasay City led to the arrest of two newly identified high-value individuals (HVIs) and the seizure of about ₱1.02 million worth of suspected shabu on Thursday night, Aug. 13. The Southern Police District (SPD) identified the suspects as Timor, 30, a vendor and resident of Barangay Baclaran, Parañaque City, and John Ashley, 25, a resident of Barangay 145, Pasay City. Police said the two were arrested at around 7:35 p.m. inside a computer shop along Sarhento Mariano Don Carlos Revilla Street in Barangay 146. Operatives of the SPD District Drug Enforcement Unit (DDEU), together with the District Intelligence Division and the Pasay City Police Station Drug Enforcement Unit, carried out the buy-bust operation. A police officer acting as poseur-buyer allegedly negotiated a drug transaction with Timor inside the shop, leading to the immediate arrest of both suspects. Recovered from Timor were one heat-sealed transparent plastic sachet and one knot-tied transparent plastic bag containing suspected shabu, along with the buy-bust money, a white envelope, and a black plastic bag. Another sachet of suspected shabu and a light-blue Android smartphone were seized from Ashley. The confiscated drugs weighed about 150 grams and had an estimated standard drug price of ₱1.02 million. Police said Timor will face complaints for violations of Sections 5 (sale) and 11 (possession) of Article II of Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. Ashley will face a complaint for violation of Section 11 (possession) of the same law. The suspects were brought to the DDEU-SPD office for documentation and processing as police prepared the criminal complaints. The SPD said the operation highlights its continuing crackdown on illegal drug activities, particularly transactions allegedly carried out inside establishments used as meeting places by suspected dealers and buyers.

Pasig court keeps P85 wage hike on hold. The Pasig City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 152 on Thursday, Aug. 13, issued a preliminary injunction placing the P85 daily minimum wage hike for workers in the National Capital Region on hold. The order, signed by Presiding Judge Marie Joyce Manongsong, granted the petitioners’ request against Wage Order No. 27, stopping its implementation pending the court’s decision on the case. The petition was filed by Readycon Trading and Construction Corp. and R-II Builders, Inc. “Accordingly, the court grants petitioners' prayer for a writ of preliminary injunction. Respondents are enjoined from implementing Wage Order No. 27 pending this court's determination of the merits of the petition for declaratory relief,” the order read. The court said that "it is to the best interest of all stakeholders that the assailed wage order be temporarily put on pause" after citing possible job losses that could result from the implementation of the minimum wage increase. “To the court's mind, this work terminations should not be easily dismissed as trivial. Losing one's employment is graver and irreversible than the temporary inability to receive additional wages,” the order read. “This, along with the other grim consequences discussed above, are precisely the reasons why this court deems that momentarily enjoining the implementation of the assailed wage order is not only legal but also just,” it added. The court said that in issuing the order, it was not recklessly transgressing Article 126 of the Labor Code, noting that it had fully recognized the interconnected interests of employers and employees in matters concerning wages. It also said that the injunction was meant to ensure that the rights of both management and labor are considered and their livelihoods sustained. In addition, the court acknowledged the possible damage or burdens that the injunctive order could cause to millions of workers across the region and deemed a P10 billion bond sufficient as an injunction bond. A temporary restraining order (TRO) was issued in late July against the implementation of the P85 daily minimum wage increase in Metro Manila, which senators criticized. The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board-National Capital Region (RTWPB-NCR) earlier issued Wage Order No. 27, which provides for an additional P85 in the daily minimum wage to be implemented in two phases -- the P60 increase took effect on July 25, while the remaining P25 increase will take effect starting January 2027. How a playboy aristocrat turned to a life dedicated to God. When living the high life, it’s almost unfathomable to consider ever leaving it all. Yet, for Javier Sartorius Milans del Bosch, the main subject of the documentary “Just Javier,” all it took was turning to God. “Just Javier,” originally titled “Solo Javier,” follows the story of a promising young athlete’s journey to the top. In his prime, he led a non-stop nightlife filled with sex, booze, and drugs while slowly making a name for himself as a paddle tennis player. Hoping to steer him on the right path, his parents sent him to the US to straighten him out. It was there that he was exposed to the homeless community of Venice Beach. He would eventually befriend a bunch of them, curious to learn their stories. Filled with a new perspective, Javier kept on his journey of self-discovery through meditation. As he went on, he was recommended to join a volunteer mission in Peru. There, he was shown a different kind of poverty altogether. During this time, while still mostly disassociated from it all, he managed to form a strong bond with the children he met during the trip. Slowly, the faith he had seemingly abandoned began to return. It came back strong enough to set him on a path dedicated to God, though his untimely death in 2006 occurred just before he was set to be ordained as a Catholic priest. While much of the Bosco Films production plays out like those mandatory Catholic School documentary viewings, it does stir up quite a bit of curiosity toward Javier’s life. Our viewing was a dubbed version that had somewhat distracting voice actors, but once you get over it, you are left lingering about how someone from such a privileged background could ever throw it all away. “Just Javier” does a great job of slowly showing us just how it played out. It leaves enough to make you reflect on how not even the shiniest trophies and the world’s greatest pleasures can satiate a spiritual thirst. Many liken Javier to a modern-day Saint Augustine for his journey. Then, there’s the touch of Jesuit influence, where most of its iconic saints like St. Ignatius of Loyola and St. Francis Xavier are known to have similar backgrounds of nobility before turning to a life of poverty in the name of God. He might even join their ranks someday, with efforts calling for Javier’s beautification. “Just Javier” is exclusively screening in Ayala Malls Cinemas.
